title_original: 「見る／見られる／見せる」を越えて──「アイヌ民族と博覧会　―150年の経験―」展（国立歴史民俗博物館）が問いかけるもの（評：吉本裕子）
editorial_title_zh: 超越“观看／被观看／展示”──国立历史民俗博物馆“阿伊努民族与博览会：150年的经验”展之质问（评：吉本裕子）

"caption": "展场风貌，“第五回内国劝业博览会”明细图", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "思考“展示”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿伊努民族代代传承的舞蹈在大阪·关西世博会上登台亮相，这一幕仍让人记忆犹新。正在位于千叶县佐仓市的国立历史民俗博物馆举办的“阿伊努民族与博览会：150年的经验”展，勾勒出了从1872年“汤岛圣堂博览会”首次展出阿伊努资料开始，到2025年“EXPO 2025 大阪·关西世博会”为止，长达约150年的阿伊努民族与博览会的关联。", "links": [{"text": "国立歴史民俗博物館", "url": "https://www.tokyoartbeat.com/venues/-/16071DF6"}, {"text": "「アイヌ民族と博覧会 ―150年の経験―」", "url": "https://www.tokyoartbeat.com/events/-/The-Ainu-and-the-Expositions-150-years-of-experience/16071-DF-6/2026-10-06"}, {"text": "「EXPO2025 大阪・関西万博」", "url": "https://www.tokyoartbeat.com/events/-/Expo-2025-Osaka-Kansai-Japan/yumeshima/2025-04-13"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/b4e5f728/65990b9e-5e00-419c-8fa7-af676acb3076.jpg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "博览会作为介绍新知识、文化与产业的场所，在近代社会的形成过程中发挥了巨大作用。另一方面，它也是一个搜集、分类并对人与物进行等级划分的场所。尤其是将有血有肉的人安置在会场内生活、将其作为观赏对象的“人类展示”，在文化人类学和历史学等领域中，一直从其与殖民地主义和种族主义的关系角度受到批判性审视。1903年“第五回内国劝业博览会”上设立的学术人类馆，将阿伊努人以及冲绳、朝鲜、台湾、印度、爪哇等地的人们置于被展示的境地（＊1），这在可以说是日本博览会史上具有象征意义的事件而被铭记。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/57710604/d3b7d5d1-06a7-48c3-a774-bb7d753b84ab.jpg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，本次展览的特点并不在于仅仅从“观看的一方”与“被观看的一方”这种关系来把握这段历史，而是将光芒投向了参与博览会的形形色色之人的经验及其关系性。从展览中浮现出来的，不仅是“被观看的一方”，有时也处于“观看”他人立场、并参与“展示”自身文化的阿伊努人的身影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本文将聚焦于本次展览所勾勒出的“观看／被观看／展示”这一多层面的经验，在探讨展览意义与课题的同时，思考基于这一历史的今日博物馆应有的形态。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/57a402bd/9790a204-b696-49bd-ac5c-eff9f9731979.jpg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌，川村则子制作的Mintara", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "阿伊努人并非只是“被观看的一方”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在思考参与博览会之人的多样经验时，值得关注的是探讨“人类展示”的本次展览第二章。“阿伊努民族的出场”这一章题，似乎体现了本次展览的姿态：即不将阿伊努人简单还原为“被观看的一方”的定位，而是去勾勒参与博览会之人的多样经验。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在本次展览中，除了工艺品、照片、明信片、书信、服装、影像等资料之外，出场者本人的话语以及对其子孙的采访也作为“声音”融入了展览之中。个体的实践与想法同“当下”相连这一点也令人印象深刻。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/6dad4653/117b7464-501b-4c27-94e0-5d9f118b23d1.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌，“第五回内国劝业博览会”海报", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "例如，对于1903年“第五回内国劝业博览会”上设立的学术人类馆，当时就存在对展示活人的批判。与此同时，展览也提及了出身十胜的阿伊努人伏根弘三（Fushine Kōzō，阿伊努名：Hotene）为了筹集维持“土人教育所”的资金而参加博览会，并进行了日语演讲。伏根在人类学家坪井正五郎的指导下承担了说明自身文化的角色，据称他并未将自己的活动仅仅视为一种奇观。从伏根的案例可以看出，尽管参与博览会是基于其本人目的，但学术人类馆中的活动却是在人类学家所设定的框架内进行的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/a543a709/cb4aa82f-d99d-4f36-b837-0959a43f4ae1.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "此外，展览还介绍了1904年自愿参加圣路易斯世博会的边泥五郎（Pete Gorō）的讲述。据称边泥与美国来场者亲密交流，回国后也一直保持书信往来。这段经历表明，个人之间已经产生了无法单靠“观看的一方”与“被观看的一方”这种关系来概括的持续交流。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "另外，参与海外博览会的背景中，也有长期在北海道从事传教活动的圣公会传教士约翰·巴切勒（John Batcheler）的存在。边泥及其他部分参与者是曾在巴切勒宅邸工作的信徒，而伏根据说也是圣公会的信徒。从这些案例可以看出，参与博览会也与通过传教士产生的人际关系和宗教网络紧密相连。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/7fbf4d12/7368713c-1ae4-4c97-8158-8e2025fea106.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌，有关日英博览会的明信片", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通过将光芒投向阿伊努人自身的诉求、以及他们与传教士、人类学家、来场者等之间的多样关系，展览勾勒出了无法仅凭“被观看的一方”这一定位来概括的“人类展示”的复杂历史样貌。不过，尽管图录中收录了本次展览制作人员等（＊2）对殖民地主义的批判性讨论，但展览本身并未充分呈现“究竟是谁将他人定位为展示对象”这一视角，其背后的权力关系显得难以察觉。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/d7491f95/77844e55-0015-4e2b-9f1d-b0cf141aeeb1.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "围绕“展示”的经验与选择", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "第二次世界大战后，在海外国际博览会一度中断举办的时期，日本以战后复兴和旅游振兴为背景在各地举办了博览会，阿伊努人也继续参与其中。虽然强调“原始”性的展示与战前如出一辙，但据说在参与方式上也逐渐出现了变化，例如阿伊努人开始自己设立小卖部或出展资料。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在第四章“阿伊努民族与博览会的去向”中，介绍了1970年大阪世博会成为传播阿伊努文化的一个契机。白老民族艺能保存会在大阪世博会上出演了“日本的节日”，与各地的乡土艺能一同披露了阿伊努舞蹈。从参与其中的女性们的“声音”中，可以得知出演世博会与白老旅游景点Porotokotan的宣传以及阿伊努舞蹈的舞台化紧密相连。另一方面，我们也需要关注阿伊努舞蹈是在“日本的节日”这一框架内得以披露的这一点。文化被“展示”的机会增加，并不一定等同于能够自主决定其展示方式与定位。演出与展示的框架是由谁、以怎样的方式设定出来的，这一问题同样至关重要。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/7f92b0bd/7c1210d0-632e-408a-a71d-0b867d6481c3.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "此外，展览还涉及了参加“东京2020奥运会及残奥会”以及“EXPO 2025 大阪·关西世博会”并在舞台上表演舞蹈的年轻一代的经验。这表明，在阿伊努人自身构建用于主体性地“展示”文化的网络的同时，新的相遇与关系性也由此诞生。同时，如果考虑到至今仍有人对展示文化抱有困惑与纠结，那么倘若也将此类讲述并呈出来，围绕“展示”的当今状况或许就能得到更具立体感的勾勒。以新方法“展示”文化的实践，固然能够动摇既有的民族形象，但这并不意味着围绕展示的非对称关系已经得到消除。受到质问的不仅是展示文化的一方，还有注视、消费并解读文化的“我们”的目光。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/d6d67fea/876475e4-58e0-4a6d-9364-a95b28a96937.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "重新审视处于“观看的一方”的主体多数派的历史与社会定位", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在此，我们想重新思考的是1903年学术人类馆中人类学家坪井正五郎的参与。有观点指出，19世纪末留学英国的坪井并非全盘接受西方的种族概念，而是试图对其所包含的东方主义进行批判性把握（＊3）。在第二章中也作了说明，即经坪井校阅的“世界人种地图”中不仅包含阿伊努、琉球、台湾的人们，也包含了“日本内地人”及欧美的人们，彼此处于同等地位。然而，被定位为种族分类的对象与作为有血有肉的人被置于博览会的展示空间之中，是不同维度的问。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/3340cfde/8affef6a-0365-4439-b7bb-d1e9849ebedc.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌，坪井正五郎制作的“世界人种地图”", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "事实上，针对学术人类馆中展示“琉球妇人”一事，冲绳曾引发抗议，但这些抗议中也包含了对与阿伊努及台湾人处于同等地位的抵触情绪，其中带有以当时社会进化论为背景的“种族主义目光”的前提（＊4）。近代的种族分类反映了西方中心主义的价值观，19世纪的进化论人类学将世界各地的人们置于“野蛮”“未开化”“文明”的进化阶段（＊5）。然而，笔者得到的印象是，本次展览并未充分说明这种种族分类与等级化思想是如何与“人类展示”相结合、并使得将特定人群作为展示对象成为可能的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个问题并未局限于过去的博览会。近代的民族学博物馆与博览会紧密相连，在博览会上展出的“异文化”资料有时会在闭幕后被增补进博物馆的收藏之中（＊6）。在博览会中孕育出的搜集、分类与展示表象的形态，与民族学博物馆的历史也是密不可分的。20世纪80年代后期以来，通过与原住民协作来开展展览制作及博物馆运营的形态之所以遭到摸索，正是源于对这段历史及其所支撑的权力关系的批判。再者，考虑到针对阿伊努民族的人类学研究与遗骨搜集历史、以及延续至当下的歧视问题，我们无法将把人作为研究与展示对象的目光作为过去的事情一笔勾销。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/c699583b/56c636a5-63ec-4ca5-b14b-0f8e13f06fce.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌，“拓殖博览会”广告", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本次展览从与他人的关系性中将参与博览会的阿伊努个体多样经验可视化，并通过提示阿伊努自身“展示”文化的视角，带来了动摇传统民族形象的契机。另一方面，在博览会历史中主要处于“观看的一方”的人们的历史和社会定位的视角，在本次展览中是否得到了充分的呈现呢？今日的博物馆不仅被要求展示阿伊努人展示了什么、又是如何被观看的，是否还被要求明确提供一个契机，去质问究竟是谁在怎样的权力关系下将他人作为展示对象，并思考这段历史是如何与当下相连的呢？多数派一方持续面对这些质问，这也将转化为：不仅将阿伊努人的主体性停留在个人意志与选择的问题上，而是从使其成为可能或对其进行制约的历史和社会条件出发对其进行重新审视。笔者在此提出的质问，同样也指向作为和人研究者观看了本次展览的自己，在此谨作自我告诫。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/10cdd249/d6d5c9b1-c527-41a6-ae32-bf15ca9b70b9.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌，世界人类风俗人偶", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "＊1──清国、朝鲜、冲绳发出了抗议之声，这些地区人们的展示被中止（松田京子《帝国的视线：博览会与异文化表象》，2003年，吉川弘文館，pp. 121–124）。 ＊2──关口由彦“人类馆是什么”，国立历史民俗博物馆、阿伊努民族文化财团编《阿伊努民族与博览会：150年的经验》，2026年，合同会社小さ子社，pp. 112-115。 ＊3──松田京子《帝国的视线：博览会与异文化表象》，2003年，吉川弘文館，p. 154。 ＊4──同上书，pp. 129–133。 ＊5──吉田宪司《文化的“发现”》，1999年，岩波書店，pp. 39–40。 ＊6──同上书，pp. 40–43。", "translated": true}]

"paragraph", "text": "博覧会は、新たな知識や文化、産業を紹介する場として近代社会の形成に大きな役割を果たしてきた。いっぽうで、それは人やモノを収集し、分類し、序列化する場でもあった。とりわけ、会場内で生身の人間を生活させ、観覧の対象とした「人間展示」は、文化人類学や歴史学等の分野において、植民地主義や人種主義との関係から批判的に検討されてきた。1903年の「第5回内国勧業博覧会」に設置された学術人類館では、アイヌをはじめ沖縄、朝鮮、台湾、インド、ジャワ等の人々が展示対象となり（＊1）、日本の博覧会史においても象徴的な出来事として記憶されている。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/57710604/d3b7d5d1-06a7-48c3-a774-bb7d753b84ab.jpg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "会場風景", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "この問題は、過去の博覧会だけにとどまらない。近代の民族学博物館は博覧会と密接に結びつき、博覧会で展示された「異文化」の資料が、閉幕後に博物館のコレクションに加えられることもあった（＊6）。博覧会で培われた収集・分類・展示表象の在り方は、民族学博物館の歴史とも切り離せないのである。1980年代後半以降、先住民族との協働による展示制作や博物館運営の在り方が模索されてきた背景には、こうした歴史と、それを支えてきた権力関係への批判がある。さらに、アイヌ民族に対する人類学的研究や遺骨収集の歴史、現在に至る差別の問題を考えれば、人々を研究・展示の対象としてきたまなざしを、過去のものとして片づけることはできない。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/c699583b/56c636a5-63ec-4ca5-b14b-0f8e13f06fce.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "会場風景、「拓殖博覧会」の広告", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本展は、博覧会に関わったアイヌ個々人の多様な経験を、他者との関係性から可視化するとともに、アイヌ自らが文化を「見せる」という視点を提示することで、従来の民族イメージを揺さぶる契機をもたらした。いっぽうで、博覧会の歴史のなかで主として「見る側」に立ってきた人々の歴史的・社会的位置を問い直す視点は、本展において十分に提示されていただろうか。今日の博物館には、アイヌの人々が何を「見せ」、どのように「見られて」きたのかを示すだけでなく、誰が、いかなる権力関係のもとで他者を展示対象としてきたのかを問い、その歴史が現在とどのようにつながっているのかを考える契機を明確に提供することも求められるのではないだろうか。こうした問いにマジョリティの側が向き合い続けることは、アイヌの人々の主体性を、個人の意思や選択の問題にとどめず、それを可能にし、あるいは制約する歴史的・社会的条件から問い直すことにもつながっている。ここに提示した問いは、和人である一研究者として本展を見た筆者自身にも向けられていることを、自戒を込めて述べておきたい。"}, article_text:
「見せる」ことを考える

大阪・関西万博において、アイヌ民族が伝承してきた舞踊が披露されたことは記憶に新しい。千葉・佐倉にある 国立歴史民俗博物館 にて開催中の 「アイヌ民族と博覧会 ―150年の経験―」 展は、1872年の「湯島聖堂博覧会」にアイヌ資料が初めて出品されてから、2025年の 「EXPO2025 大阪・関西万博」 に至るまで、およそ150年にわたるアイヌ民族と博覧会の関わりを描き出している。

博覧会は、新たな知識や文化、産業を紹介する場として近代社会の形成に大きな役割を果たしてきた。いっぽうで、それは人やモノを収集し、分類し、序列化する場でもあった。とりわけ、会場内で生身の人間を生活させ、観覧の対象とした「人間展示」は、文化人類学や歴史学等の分野において、植民地主義や人種主義との関係から批判的に検討されてきた。1903年の「第5回内国勧業博覧会」に設置された学術人類館では、アイヌをはじめ沖縄、朝鮮、台湾、インド、ジャワ等の人々が展示対象となり（＊1）、日本の博覧会史においても象徴的な出来事として記憶されている。

しかし、本展の特徴は、こうした歴史を「見る側」と「見られる側」という関係からのみとらえるのではなく、博覧会に関わった多様な人々の経験や、その関係性に光を当てている点にある。展示から浮かび上がるのは、「見られる側」にとどまらず、ときに他者を「見る」立場にもなり、自らの文化を「見せる」ことにも関わってきたアイヌの人々の姿である。

本稿では、本展が描き出す「見る／見られる／見せる」という重層的な経験に着目しながら、展示の意義と課題を検討するとともに、その歴史を踏まえた今日の博物館の在り方について考えてみたい。

「見られる側」だけではなかったアイヌの人々

博覧会に関わった人々の多様な経験を考えるうえで、注目したいのは「人間展示」を扱う本展の第2章である。「アイヌ民族の出場」という章題には、アイヌを「見られる側」という位置づけに還元せず、博覧会に関わった人々の多様な経験を描き出そうとする本展の姿勢が表れているように思われた。

本展では、工芸品・写真・絵はがき・書簡・衣装・映像などの資料に加え、出場者本人の言葉やその子孫へのインタビューが「声」として展示に組み込まれている。個々人の営みや思いが「現在」へと接続されている点も印象的であった。

たとえば、1903年の「第5回内国勧業博覧会」に設置された学術人類館に対しては、当時から人間を展示することへの批判があった。そのいっぽうで、十勝出身のアイヌ・伏根弘三（ふしねこうぞう、アイヌ名：ホテネ）が、「土人教育所」の維持のための寄付を募る目的で博覧会に参加し、日本語による演説を行ったことが取り上げられている。伏根は人類学者・坪井正五郎の指導のもとで自文化について説明する役割を担い、自らの活動をたんなる見世物とはとらえていなかったという。伏根の事例からは、博覧会への参加が本人の目的に基づくものであったいっぽうで、学術人類館での活動は人類学者によって設定された枠組みのなかで行われていたことがうかがえる。

加えて、1904年のセントルイス万博に自ら志願して参加した辺泥五郎（ぺてごろう）の語りも紹介されている。辺泥は米国人来場者と親しく交流し、帰国後も文通を続けていたという。その経験は、「見る側」と「見られる側」という関係だけではとらえきれない、個人間の継続的な交流が生まれていたことを物語っている。

また、海外博覧会への参加の背景には、北海道で長年宣教活動を行っていた聖公会の宣教師ジョン・バチェラーの存在もあった。辺泥やほかの参加者の一部はバチェラー邸で働いていた信者であり、伏根も聖公会の信徒であったという。こうした事例からは、博覧会への参加が、宣教師を介した人間関係や宗教的ネットワークとも結びついていたことがうかがえる。

アイヌ自身の目的や、宣教師、人類学者、来場者などとの多様な関係に光を当てることで、「見られる側」という位置づけだけではとらえきれない「人間展示」の複雑な歴史のありようを描き出している。ただし、図録では本展の制作担当者ら（＊2）による植民地主義への批判的な議論がなされているものの、展示では誰が他者を展示対象として位置づけたのかという視点が十分に示されておらず、その背景にある権力関係は見えにくかった。

「見せる」ことをめぐる経験と選択

第二次世界大戦後、海外では国際博覧会の開催がしばらく途絶えるなか、日本では戦後復興や観光振興を背景に各地で博覧会が開催され、アイヌの人々も引き続き参加した。戦前と同様に「原始」性を強調する展示が続くいっぽうで、次第にアイヌ自身が売店を設けたり、資料を出品したりするなど、参加の在り方にも変化が見られるようになったという。

第4章「アイヌ民族と博覧会のゆくえ」では、1970年の大阪万博がアイヌ文化の発信におけるひとつの契機となったことが紹介されている。白老民族芸能保存会は大阪万博で「日本のまつり」に出演し、各地の郷土芸能とともにアイヌ舞踊を披露した。参加した女性たちの「声」からは、万博への出演が白老の観光地ポロトコタンの周知や、アイヌ舞踊の舞台化とも結びついていったことがわかる。いっぽうで、アイヌ舞踊が「日本のまつり」という枠組みのなかで披露されたことにも目を向けたい。文化を「見せる」機会が広がることと、その見せ方や位置づけを自ら決定できることは、必ずしも同義ではない。公演や展示の枠組みが誰によって、どのように設定されてきたのかという問題も重要である。

さらに、「東京2020オリンピック・パラリンピック競技大会」や「EXPO2025 大阪・関西万博」に参加し舞台で舞踊を披露した若い世代の経験も取り上げられた。文化を主体的に「見せる」ためのネットワークをアイヌ自らが構築しながら、新たな出会いや関係性が生まれてきたことが示されている。同時に、文化を見せることに戸惑いや葛藤を抱く人々がいまも存在していることを踏まえるならば、そのような語りも併せて提示されていれば、「見せる」ことをめぐる今日的な状況がより立体的に描き出されたのではないだろうか。新たな方法で文化を「見せる」という営みは、既存の民族イメージを揺るがすことにつながるいっぽう、展示をめぐる非対称な関係が解消されたことを意味するわけではない。問われているのは、文化を見せる側だけではなく、それを見つめ、消費し、解釈する「われわれ」のまなざしでもある。

「見る側」に立つマジョリティの歴史的・社会的位置を問い直す

ここで改めて考えたいのが、1903年の学術人類館における人類学者・坪井正五郎の関わりである。19世紀末に英国へ留学した坪井は、西洋の人種概念をそのまま受容したわけではなく、そこに含まれるオリエンタリズムを批判的にとらえようとしていたことが指摘されている（＊3）。第2章でも、坪井が校閲した「世界人種地図」には、アイヌや琉球、台湾の人々だけでなく、「日本内地人」や欧米の人々も含まれ、それぞれが同列に示されていたことが説明されている。しかし、人種分類の対象として位置づけられることと、生身の人間として博覧会の展示空間に置かれることは、異なる次元の問題である。

実際、学術人類館で「琉球婦人」が展示されたことに対して沖縄から抗議が起こったが、その抗議にはアイヌや台湾の人々と同列に位置づけられることへの反発も含まれ、当時の社会進化論を背景とした「人種主義的まなざし」を前提とする側面があった（＊4）。近代の人種分類には西欧中心的な価値観が反映され、19世紀の進化論的人類学は世界の人々を「野蛮」「未開」「文明」という発展段階に位置づけてきた（＊5）。しかし、本展では、こうした人種分類や序列化の思想が「人間展示」とどのように結びつき、特定の人々を展示対象とすることを可能にしたのかについて、十分に説明されていない印象を受けた。

この問題は、過去の博覧会だけにとどまらない。近代の民族学博物館は博覧会と密接に結びつき、博覧会で展示された「異文化」の資料が、閉幕後に博物館のコレクションに加えられることもあった（＊6）。博覧会で培われた収集・分類・展示表象の在り方は、民族学博物館の歴史とも切り離せないのである。1980年代後半以降、先住民族との協働による展示制作や博物館運営の在り方が模索されてきた背景には、こうした歴史と、それを支えてきた権力関係への批判がある。さらに、アイヌ民族に対する人類学的研究や遺骨収集の歴史、現在に至る差別の問題を考えれば、人々を研究・展示の対象としてきたまなざしを、過去のものとして片づけることはできない。

本展は、博覧会に関わったアイヌ個々人の多様な経験を、他者との関係性から可視化するとともに、アイヌ自らが文化を「見せる」という視点を提示することで、従来の民族イメージを揺さぶる契機をもたらした。いっぽうで、博覧会の歴史のなかで主として「見る側」に立ってきた人々の歴史的・社会的位置を問い直す視点は、本展において十分に提示されていただろうか。今日の博物館には、アイヌの人々が何を「見せ」、どのように「見られて」きたのかを示すだけでなく、誰が、いかなる権力関係のもとで他者を展示対象としてきたのかを問い、その歴史が現在とどのようにつながっているのかを考える契機を明確に提供することも求められるのではないだろうか。こうした問いにマジョリティの側が向き合い続けることは、アイヌの人々の主体性を、個人の意思や選択の問題にとどめず、それを可能にし、あるいは制約する歴史的・社会的条件から問い直すことにもつながっている。ここに提示した問いは、和人である一研究者として本展を見た筆者自身にも向けられていることを、自戒を込めて述べておきたい。

＊1──清国、朝鮮、沖縄から抗議の声が上がり、これらの地域の人々の展示は中止された（松田京子『帝国の視線―博覧会と異文化表象』、2003、吉川弘文館、pp. 121–124）。 ＊2──関口由彦「人類館とは何か」、国立歴史民俗博物館・アイヌ民族文化財団編『アイヌ民族と博覧会―150年の経験』、2026、合同会社小さ子社、pp. 112-115。 ＊3──松田京子『帝国の視線―博覧会と異文化表象』、2003、吉川弘文館、p. 154。 ＊4──同書、pp. 129–133。 ＊5──吉田憲司『文化の「発見」』1999、岩波書店、pp. 39–40。 ＊6──同書、pp. 40–43。

article_text:
Watermelon Pictures co-founders Badie Ali and Hamza Ali , who had a high-profile 2025-26 Oscars season with their International Feature Film nominee The Voice Of Hind Rajab and shortlisted titles Palestine 36 and All That’s Left Of You , are back on the awards trail with documentary American Doctor .

The film centers on three American physicians of differing backgrounds who volunteered their services in besieged hospitals in Gaza, treating Palestinian children grievously injured in Israel’s sustained bombardment and invasion of the occupied territory.

The pair were at the ninth edition of Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival (GFF) last week with the film, directed by Oscar-nominee and Emmy-winner Poh Si Teng, where it won the Cinema For Humanity Audience Award. Their company is also the North American distributor of Who Killed Alex Odeh? , about the murder of the American Palestinian activist in California in 1985, which featured in GFF’s Feature Documentary Competition this year.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Inaugural West Hollywood Human Rights Film Festival To Showcase Oscar-Contending Documentaries, 20th Anniversary Screening Of 'Blood Diamond'

Watermelon Pictures Acquires North American Distribution Rights To Sara Ishaq's 'The Station'

These are just a couple of examples from Watermelon Pictures’ growing slate that champions stories from Palestine and beyond , as well as amplifies “marginalized voices that wouldn’t typically have a platform.”

Deadline caught up with the two Ali brothers at GFF’s Festival Plaza by the Red Sea to talk about their future vision for Watermelon Pictures, the impact of The Voice Of Hind Rajab ‘s success, releasing American Doctor , and the ideological shift in Hollywood when it comes to telling stories about Palestine.

“We’ve been seeing a renaissance with a lot of the A-listers,” said Badie. “There’s a shift in momentum. You’re seeing people come out and start working with us because of our stance, not in spite of it, so it’s unprecedented to say the least.”

You can read the interview below, which has been edited for length and clarity.

DEADLINE: You founded Watermelon Pictures in 2024, and in just two years, you’ve expanded your slate with so many great films. What’s your vision for the upcoming few years?

HAMZA: We are going to continue on this route of amplifying underrepresented voices, specifically from the region and beyond, as well as marginalized voices that wouldn’t typically have a platform.

We’re very excited to be here in El Gouna. We are releasing El Sett in December, which is very resonant. We’re also working on a development slate, which is going to be more about reaching mainstream audiences and humanizing our people through entertainment.

DEADLINE: Speaking of mainstream audiences, do you have plans to start distributing outside of North America?

HAMZA: We act as an international sales agent, so we do sub-distribute to other distributors in different regions, but eventually, we would like to be more of a global distribution company.

DEADLINE: I’d like to talk a bit about The Voice Of Hind Rajab. Did you envision its global resonance and the Oscar-nomination?

HAMZA: With Kaouther’s vision and obviously the story itself, which is powerful and sad, we weren’t super surprised by the success the film had. Of course, we’re happy that it received a nomination because it amplifies the reach of the film. Film distribution is very tricky, but we’re happy to see where it landed.

BADIE: In addition, we had two other films that were shortlisted alongside The Voice of Hind Rajab . One was Palestine 36 and the other was All That’s Left Of You . Last year, three out of the fifteen shortlisted films were Palestinian, which speaks to the cause and the moment. The good thing is that audiences and members of the Academy are starting to see the importance of this work and how these films have a greater impact on humanity.

DEADLINE: I attended a screening of All That’s Left Of You with its director Cherien Dabis and she was talking about the difficulty of getting people to watch films about Palestine. What do you think works and what doesn’t in terms of getting a big audience to see these films?

BADIE: We put such an emphasis on the Academy Awards and the campaign to push for it because that’s one of the best ways to amplify beyond our community. Our communities typically do come out to see these films, but we need more mainstream audiences.

Obviously, foreign language is a challenge, but we’re trying. The Voice of Hind Rajab getting nominated opened the door for a Hulu sale. Hulu taking it has opened another door for people who have no idea about the issue and are now being more exposed to the content. All this stuff works in tandem. That’s what Hamza and I were talking about. Our next development slate is a little bit more commercial, maybe English language for our region. That again, opens a door to our culture that makes content more accessible.

HAMZA: Part of what we do is trying to get these diverse audiences. Our marketing approach is four quadrant. We’re trying to get as wide of an audience out as possible, and we are seeing that. Right now, we’re releasing American Doctor and we’ve been happy to see that the audiences are extremely diverse. That’s the goal. We’re going to continue to do that through the content, and distribution strategy.

DEADLINE: You had an interesting approach to the American Doctor marketing campaign , in which you provided healthcare workers free tickets to screenings. Can you tell me about the thought process behind that?

HAMZA: We wanted to stay true to our ethos. It’s more than just film and entertainment. It was our way of honoring the work of the healthcare workers. It was such a beautiful sight to see these nurses, doctors and EMTs coming out in their scrubs and their white coats, and wearing scrub caps in the theater. Just another way of making cinema with a purpose.

DEADLINE: You’ve worked with a lot of top directors like Kaouther Ben Hania, Annemarie Jacir, and Cherien Dabis to name a few. Who else is on your wish list?

HAMZA: We have some exciting ones on the horizon already that haven’t been announced, so you’ll see soon. We’re expanding and broadening our scope. Our goal is to bring in more of these adjacent causes or aligned people within the industry. Maybe people who have been a bit blacklisted for the wrong reasons, and making sure that they have a soft landing with us, and that will give them not only a home but a really strong place for their films to debut.

BADIE: We’ve been seeing a renaissance with a lot of the A-listers. When people think of Hollywood, they think it has a certain ideology. But the reality is most of the people who work within Hollywood are actually aligned. There’s a shift in momentum. You’re seeing people come out and start working with us because of our stance, not in spite of it, so it’s unprecedented to say the least.

DEADLINE: Do you see hope with more A-list Hollywood actors like Javier Bardem, Mark Ruffalo , Joaquin Phoenix and Rooney Mara becoming more involved in supporting Palestinian stories?

HAMZA: Absolutely. One example I’d like to highlight is Melissa Barrera. She’s amazing, and she was before her time with the whole Scream situation .

Now, most of the cast are coming out saying we should have stood by her, like Jenna Ortega did. And another example, not film-related, but Macklemore’s situation with Ed Sheeran. I think Ed Sheeran made a huge mistake, not only by not supporting Palestine, but by also censoring his fellow artists. People don’t want to see censorship, and so, that’s where we come in and say, ‘You have a home here with us.’

title_original: The Film Comment Podcast: Stealing Time
editorial_excerpt_zh: 本期嘉宾：凯莉·雷查德（Kelly Reichardt）、肯特·琼斯（Kent Jones）和卢西奥·卡斯特罗（Lucio Castro）做客NYFF63，探讨电影与其他艺术的时光性、职业艺术家的挑战等话题
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "今年NYFF的三部影片探讨了日常生活与艺术的交汇点，讲述了多位艺术家的故事：他们为创作热情争取时间和空间的努力，屡屡遭到日常琐碎劳累的阻挠或挫败。在肯特·琼斯（Kent Jones）改编自亚瑟·施尼茨勒（Arthur Schnitzler）中篇小说的《Late Fame》中，一位昔日的纽约诗人（如今是一名邮局员工）因一群二十多岁、怀揣文学梦的年轻诗人群体的突然关注而飘飘然。在凯莉·雷查德（Kelly Reichardt）以1970年代为背景的《The Mastermind》中，一个漫无目的的艺术院校辍学生在当地一家博物馆实施了一起滑稽而草率的抢劫，仿佛是在寻求逃离平庸的中产阶级家庭生活。而在卢西奥·卡斯特罗（Lucio Castro）的《Drunken Noodles》中，一名艺术生在纽约度过了一个夏天，围绕着绘画、诗歌和写作经历了一系列巧合且充满情欲的遭遇。每部影片都在探讨这样一个主题：艺术的创作与消费如何迫使生活进入一种与现代世界格格不入的节奏。", "links": [{"text": "Late Fame", "url": "https://www.filmlinc.org/nyff2025/films/late-fame/"}, {"text": "The Mastermind", "url": "https://www.filmlinc.org/nyff2025/films/the-mastermind/"}, {"text": "Drunken Noodles", "url": "https://www.filmlinc.org/nyff2025/films/drunken-noodles/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "上周日在NYFF，琼斯、雷查德和卡斯特罗与《Film Comment》编辑德维卡·吉里什（Devika Girish）和克林顿·克鲁特（Clinton Krute）一同展开对话，探讨了电影与其他艺术的时光性、职业艺术家的挑战，以及他们新片背后的精湛工艺。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Three films in this year’s NYFF lineup explore the intersections of quotidian life and the arts, following artists whose efforts to make time and space for their creative passions are thwarted or frustrated by the grind of the everyday. In Kent Jones’s Late Fame , adapted from an Arthur Schnitzler novella, a once-upon-a-time New York poet (and now a postal worker) is intoxicated by the sudden attentions of a coterie of twentysomething wannabe poets. In Kelly Reichardt’s The Mastermind , set in the 1970s, an aimless art-school dropout executes a comically sloppy heist at a local museum, as if seeking escape from his banal, bourgeois family life. And in Lucio Castro’s Drunken Noodles , an art student spends a summer in New York, having a series of serendipitous and erotic encounters around painting, poetry, and writing. Each film dwells in how both the making and consuming of art can force life into a pace incompatible with that of the modern world.

Last Sunday at NYFF, Jones, Reichardt, and Castro joined Film Comment editors Devika Girish and Clinton Krute for a conversation exploring the temporality of cinema versus the other arts, the challenge of being a working artist, and the exquisite craft behind their new films.

title_original: In Postwar Rural France, Alexander Calder Found Respite from Pressures of Fame and a Chance to Dream Big
editorial_title_zh: 在战后法国乡村，亚历山大·考尔德摆脱了成名的压力，并找到了放飞宏大梦想的机会
editorial_excerpt_zh: “他利用在那里的生活来平复神经系统，”这位艺术家的孙子、考尔德基金会主席亚历山大·S·C·罗尔（Alexander S. C. Rower）说道。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果你曾长时间、仔细地凝视过亚历山大·考尔德（Alexander Calder）用铁丝悬挂、涂成纯色的叶状金属造型制成的动态雕塑（mobiles），你大概会明白，它们既关乎其雕塑形态与剪影，也同样关乎它们周围流动的空气、光线、阴影和自然。它们颤动、漂移，与周围大气中捉摸不透的变化嬉戏，让看不见的微风变得清晰可辨。考尔德时而精致、时而庞大的雕塑，正与我们身边的巨大自然力量融为一体。", "links": [{"text": "Alexander Calder", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/alexander-calder/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在巴黎豪瑟与沃斯画廊（Hauser & Wirth），其中几件雕塑目前正在展出（展期至12月19日），展览名为“考尔德：弗朗索瓦一世”（Calder: François Premier）。这场展览聚焦于这位已故艺术家在1953年至1954年从美国重返法国的时期，其中包括几件已逾70年未曾公开露面的动态雕塑：《莱格拉内特》（Les Granettes，1953年）和《帕特尼动态雕塑》（The Putney Mobile，1954年）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与它们一同展出的还有楼上画廊中满满一室大胆、抽象且具象的水粉画，这些作品创作于普罗旺斯地区艾克斯附近一个名为莱格拉内特（Les Granettes，1953年的动态雕塑便是在此创作并以其命名）的小村庄，以及卢瓦尔河谷另一个小村庄萨谢（Saché，现为艺术家驻留地）的一栋17世纪住宅之间。其中较为具象的水粉画包含了神秘的意象，如金字塔、脉动的类行星球体，甚至还有几只骆驼。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在阔别法国20年之后，谈及这次法国之行，考尔德说：“我似乎开发出了某种新东西。”他“主要”的家和工作室依然扎根于康涅狄格州罗克斯伯里，但他最终在萨谢生活和工作，直至1976年逝世。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“考尔德在1953年重返法国，对于理解他的晚期创作至关重要。重回故地极大地鼓舞了他，也启发了他，”他的孙子兼考尔德基金会主席亚历山大·S·C·罗尔（Alexander S. C. Rower）在画廊放映的一部纪录片中说道。“以一种前所未有方式，他直接在金属上进行绘画：全尺寸地制作、焊接、手工打造这些作品，这在以前是没有过的。这是一个非凡的时刻，诞生了具有极其丰富词汇的奇妙作品。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/CALDEiv-HWP-2610-NB-view05-hires.jpg?w=400", "alt": "艺术画廊的内部景观，悬挂着一件动态雕塑，墙上有抽象画作，一人正看着一个玻璃展柜。", "caption": "“考尔德：弗朗索瓦一世”展览现场，2026年，位于巴黎豪瑟与沃斯画廊。摄影：尼古拉斯·布拉瑟（Nicolas Brasseur）；艺术品：©2026 纽约及巴黎考尔德基金会与ADAGP / 鸣谢纽约考尔德基金会及纽约艺术资源", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但是，究竟是什么最初把考尔德带到了法国乡村？这个地方又如何改变了他的创作方式？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了探究究竟，ARTnews采访了罗尔，他的祖父去世时他年仅13岁。罗尔对我进行了一次简短而“充满活力”的解读，他最初错误地断定我年轻时曾是一名雕塑家，随后又修正了这一预测，称我以后可能会成为雕塑家，大概在60多岁的时候。接着，罗尔从考尔德的战后故事讲起。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“背后的故事是，二战期间，考尔德的所有朋友都试图来到美国避难，”他告诉我。考尔德曾写信给国务院，成功敦促他们接纳来自欧洲的艺术家，例如费尔南·莱热（Fernand Léger）和安德烈·马松（André Masson）。他最终收留了马松及其年幼的家人，他们全都睡在考尔德位于康涅狄格州的谷仓工作室里。战后，马松坚持要考尔德去普罗旺斯地区艾克斯，但这并不需要费多大口舌。考尔德带着妻子路易莎（Louisa）和两个女儿收拾好行囊，到1953年便加入了他们在法国南部的老友行列。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "那年晚些时候，考尔德一家发现了法国中部的萨谢，另一位朋友（后来成为其女婿）法美记者让·戴维森（Jean Davidson）当时正住在那里。不久，考尔德用三件动态雕塑作交换，在戴维森的土地上买下了萨谢的一栋房子。从那时起，“萨谢非常自然地演变成了这个中心。他们的孙辈在那里出生，这里成了他们的家园，”罗尔说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了简洁和清晰起见，这段对话经过了编辑和删节。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARTnews：法国乡村对考尔德而言有什么特别之处和启发意义，从而可能启发了我们在巴黎看到的这些作品？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "亚历山大·S·C·罗尔：我不会说法国或乡村启发了他。他创作的作品并非与他在那个村庄和地区的亲身经历有关。他利用在那里的生活来平复神经系统。当他在1953年出现时，他已经是一个超级大人物了，有着接不完的委托。他是这样一个见多识广的人物，因而需要一份宁静。这正是萨谢真正深刻代表的东西。吸引他的并不是当地的建筑或城堡。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "用考尔德自己的话说，他说他试图回到“中世纪”——他指的是一些简单的事情，比如去某个有木烤炉烤面包的地方，或者另一个养着一群山羊、能自己做奶酪的地方。他喜欢那些生活中可能遭遇更多挑战、但也更有真实感的人，而且他觉得自已也是这样的人。他在成长过程中一无所有。他的母亲是一位画家。他的父亲是一位雕塑家。他不得不靠自己白手起家。所以法国的乡村，至今仍然很像那样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种远离尘嚣的简单生活是否改变了他的创作？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "它确实改变了他的作品，但并没有启发他的作品。我想说的是，凭借广阔无垠的天空，他当时有机会梦想更大尺度的雕塑。他也一直在取得成功。到1962年，他找到了一家大型工业铁工厂来制作他的主要作品。他在康涅狄格州已经有一家较小的工厂来制作所有的大型作品，而现在他需要在法国也有一家，最大的一些作品正是在法国制作的。对于1963年完成的第一批作品，它们全都是为他自己制作的。他委托制作了七件户外雕塑，因为他有足够的资金去创造他想创造的东西。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/CALDE146361-AR6228042.jpg?w=400", "alt": "一件带有红色和黑色造型的落地动态雕塑。它放置在一处林木繁茂的区域。", "caption": "亚历山大·考尔德（Alexander Calder），《Les Granettes》，1953年。©2026 Calder Foundation, New York and ADAGP, Paris/Courtesy Calder Foundation, New York and Art Resource, New York", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他在法国的工作室是什么样的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
If you’ve ever looked long and slow enough at Alexander Calder ’s mobiles made of wire-suspended, leaf-like metal shapes painted solid colors, you likely know that they are as much about their sculptural form and silhouette as they are about the breathing air, light, shadow, and nature all around them. They shiver, drift, and play with the unpredictable whims of the surrounding atmosphere, making the invisible ether newly visible. Calder’s alternately delicate and massive sculptures are in communion with much larger forces around us.

At Hauser & Wirth in Paris, several of these sculptures are now on view (until December 19) in the exhibition titled “Calder: François Premier.” The show focuses on the late artist’s return to France from the US from 1953 to 1954 and includes a few mobiles that haven’t been seen in over 70 years: Les Granettes (1953) and The Putney Mobile (1954).

They are joined by an upstairs gallery full of bold, abstract, and figurative gouaches made between a small hamlet near Aix-en-Provence, called Les Granettes (where the 1953 mobile was made and named for), and a 17th-century home in Saché, another hamlet in the Loire Valley, now an artist residency. The more figurative gouaches include mysterious imagery such as pyramids, pulsing, planet-like orbs and even some camels.

“I seemed to develop something new,” Calder said of this sojourn to France after a 20-year absence. His “main” home and studio remained anchored in Roxbury, Connecticut, but he ultimately spent time living and working in Saché until his death in 1976.

“Calder’s return to France in 1953 is essential in understanding his late period. He was really emboldened and really inspired by being back,” Alexander S. C. Rower, his grandson and president of the Calder Foundation, says in a film screened at the gallery. “In really an unprecedented way, he was drawing directly on the metal: fabricating, welding, crafting the works into existence in full-scale, and that didn’t happen before. It was an extraordinary moment, with fantastic works of tremendous vocabulary.”

But what had brought Calder to the French countryside in the first place, and how did the place change how he worked?

To find out, ARTnews spoke with Rower, who was 13 when his grandfather died. After he completed a quick, “energetic reading” on me, which first mistakenly concluded I had been a sculptor in my youth but was amended to predict I would become one later, possibly in my 60s, Rower started with recounting Calder’s postwar story.

“The backstory is that during WWII, all of Calder’s friends were trying to come to America and be refugees,” he told me. Calder wrote to the State Department and successfully urged them to let in artists from Europe, such as Fernand Léger and André Masson. He eventually housed Masson and his young family, who all slept in Calder’s Connecticut barn-studio. After the war, Masson insisted Calder come to Aix-en-Provence, but it didn’t take much convincing. With his wife, Louisa, and their two daughters, Calder packed their things and joined their friends in southern France by 1953.

Later that year, the Calders discovered Saché in central France, where another friend (and later son-in-law) was living: the French-American journalist Jean Davidson. Calder soon bought a house in Saché on Davidson’s land, in exchange for three mobiles. From that moment on, “Saché just very naturally evolves into this hub. They have grandchildren there, and it becomes their homestead,” Rower said.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for concision and clarity.

ARTnews: What was special and inspiring about the French countryside to Calder, that might have led to the works we’re seeing here in Paris?

Alexander S. C. Rower: I wouldn’t say that France, or the countryside, was inspiring to him. He wasn’t making works related to what he was experiencing in the village and region. He was using being there to quiet his nervous system. He’s already a super famous guy when he shows up in 1953, and he has lots and lots of commissions. He’s this worldly character, and he needs to have quietude. That’s what Saché really deeply represents. It wasn’t the architecture, the chateaux in the region.

In Calder’s own words, he said he was trying to return to the ‘medieval‘—he’s talking about simple things, like going to this one place with a wood oven for baking bread, and another place that has this flock of goats and they’re making cheese. He liked the people that had maybe more challenges in life, but also had more authenticity, and he felt he was that way. He grew up with absolutely no money. His mom was a painter. His dad was a sculptor. He had to fend for himself. So the countryside in France, it’s still quite like that.

Did that simpler life away from it all change his work?

It definitely changed his work, but didn’t inspire his work. I’d say that he then had the chance with the big open skies to dream about bigger sculpture. He also was achieving success. By 1962, he found a big industrial iron works to execute his major works. He already had a smaller one in Connecticut that was making all the big works, and now he needed one in France, and the very biggest works were executed here in France. For that first group of works completed in 1963, they were all made for his own account. He commissioned seven outdoor sculptures, because he had enough money to make what he wanted to make.

What was his studio in France like?

The wagon shed, or remise , he converted to his studio was a very small space. A highly productive space. He made so many works there of the late period. Some of the 1950s, but mostly ’60s. Most of the sculpture made in the 1960s was made in that studio. Everything else before that was made in Connecticut, which was his number one studio.

When he arrived in France in 1953, he made four outdoor sculptures, standing mobiles that you put in your garden, one of which was Les Granettes (1953). He made lots of smaller works, but he didn’t make any big sculptures [in France that year].

And yet he started to think more about making large-scale works in Saché?

Saché is this little town where Henri de Balzac used to go and write, and it’s very flat. There’s nothing mountainous in the region, and the idea of monumental sculptures coming up out of the landscape is pretty obvious. It’s big sky country. Maybe the sky, you could say, was inspiring, because a big dynamic black form against the sky is terrific.

Why did you love about this place as a child?

Seeing Calder hard at work in France was a great pleasure. To go to the foundry, and see how he talked to the guys. He loved the guys that helped him execute his works. He wasn’t dismissive. He wasn’t offhand. He wasn’t at a distance. He was really connected with them. He gave them all gouaches and stuff. The welder was the guy he really liked. He’d come bring him a bottle of wine and talk about welding.

I wonder whether they kept any of those artworks he gave them.

They’ve all sold them. They’ve all come to market, and the grandchildren have sold them for education or whatever. Calder would have loved that. It’s just as it should be.

article_text:
Barbara Barrie , the Oscar-, Emmy- and Tony-nominated actress who starred in the original production of “Company” and in films including “Breaking Away,” died Wednesday in Manhattan. She was 95.

Her daughter confirmed her death to the New York Times and said Barrie’s death was medically assisted following a terminal cancer diagnosis.

On stage, Barrie made her Broadway debut in 1955 in “The Wooden Dish,” and went on to perform in roles across Broadway and off for more than 60 years until she took her last bow in “Significant Other.” She starred in 1976’s “California Suite,” 1958’s “The Crucible,” and in both “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” and “The Taming of the Shrew” from 1958-1959. She was, most notably, a member of the original Broadway cast of “Company,” Stephen Sondheim’s acclaimed 1970s musical. She was nominated for a Tony for best featured actress in a musical for the role of Sarah.

Related Stories

Guillermo del Toro, Diego Luna, Alfonso Cuarón to Attend Morelia Fest as Director Daniela Michel Sees Shift to Intimate Mexican Stories

Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s ‘Jengira’s Magnificent Dream,’ With Tilda Swinton, Boarded by ‘Triangle of Sadness’ Mexican Co-Producer Piano

On screen, Barrie made her film debut in “Giant” in 1956, and went on to star in 1964’s “One Potato, Two Potato,” for which she won the best actress award at the Cannes Film Festival. In 1979, she starred in “Breaking Away,” which was nominated for five Oscars. She earned a best supporting actress nod for her role. On television, Barrie appeared on shows including “The Defenders,” “Naked City,” “Twilight Zone,” “The Alfred Hitchcock Hour,” “Barney Miller” and “Suddenly Susan.” She earned Emmy nominations for the TV adaptation of “Breaking Away,” as well as for her appearances on “Law & Order” and “Law & Order: SVU.”

Barrie was born on May 23, 1931, in Chicago, and grew up in Texas. She graduated from the University of Texas in 1952 with a major in drama.

Barrie was diagnosed with rectal cancer in the early 90s, and wrote two books about her battle with the illness in an effort to reduce the stigma: “Second Act” in 1997 and “Don’t Die of Embarrassment” in 1999. Years later, in 2014, she announced that she had the degenerative disease idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

In addition to her daughter, she is survived by her son, Aaron Harnick, and three granddaughters. Her husband, Jay Harnick, died in 2007.

article_text:
French police investigating the theft of two paintings by Pierre-Auguste Renoir from a museum on the French Riviera believe the suspects were preparing to rob another institution, the Fondation Maeght in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, prosecutors said Monday.

The investigation led to the recovery of the two paintings, valued together at around $4.6 million, and the arrest of six people last week. Four men have since been charged, including two who remain in pretrial detention, according to Le Figaro , citing Agence France -Presse. Related Articles Rare Cache of Ancient Roman Sculptures Discovered at Chartres Codex Azcatitlan Goes on View in Mexico City, as Culture Ministry Continues Centuries-Long Quest for Repatriation

The paintings, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Femme au puits ( Woman at the Well ), were stolen from the Musée Renoir in Cagnes-sur-Mer on September 8. At around 5:50 a.m., two men cut through a fence and broke a window to enter the museum, housed in the artist’s former home. Using a saber saw, they removed four paintings from the walls in approximately two minutes before an alarm sounded. They abandoned two of the works and fled with the other two.

A cover left behind by the thieves provided investigators with DNA evidence that led them to a 29-year-old man from the Var department who was already known to police. Investigators subsequently identified a second suspect, a 41-year-old man living in Corsica.

“We were very clearly dealing with the repetition of a criminal project,” Eric Antonetti, director of the Alpes-Maritimes judicial police, said at a press conference, according to Le Figaro . Fearing another burglary was imminent, investigators moved to arrest the suspects on October 7.

Police first planned to wait until they could recover the paintings before making arrests. But the investigation took an unexpected turn on October 3, when officers observed the younger suspect visiting the Fondation Maeght, a major modern art institution whose collection includes works by Joan Miró, Alberto Giacometti, and Marc Chagall.

Police also observed a meeting between the principal suspect and an art dealer described by investigators as having a history of working with known forgers. Nevertheless, authorities believe the original theft was opportunistic rather than commissioned.

“The preferred hypothesis is that there was no sponsor, a priori, of the theft,” Antonetti said.

The following day, investigators recovered the two Renoirs from a house in Clermont-l’Hérault, where they had been concealed behind a false wall constructed from bricks and plasterboard. The hiding place was disclosed by a third suspect during questioning.

Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said the paintings were in relatively good condition, although both sustained damage during the burglary. They have since been transferred to the Interdisciplinary Center for Heritage Conservation and Restoration in Marseille for examination under the supervision of the Musée d’Orsay. France’s Culture Ministry said the works would eventually return to the Musée Renoir.

The case comes as French museums face renewed scrutiny over security following a series of high-profile thefts, most notably the October 2025 robbery of the Louvre, in which thieves escaped with crown jewels valued at more than $100 million . Those jewels have yet to be recovered.

article_text:
Fili di rame, metalli, superfici sottili, volti e figure emergono da una materia in continua trasformazione. Nelle opere di Marisa Merz (Torino, 1926 – 2019) la forma si definisce anche attraverso gli intervalli, le aperture e le distanze tra gli elementi. Il vuoto partecipa alla costruzione dell’opera: separa e connette, modifica la percezione, lascia spazio a interpretazioni differenti. Attorno a questa relazione tra presenza e assenza si sviluppa La danza delle ore , il grande progetto espositivo curato da Chiara Bertola, Sébastien Delot, Francesco Manacorda, Beatrice Merz, Chiara Parisi e Marianna Vecellio che si articola tra Fondazione Merz, Castello di Rivoli e GAM – Galleria Civica d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea di Torino. La mostra in corso fino al 4 aprile 2027, con il patrocinio del Ministero della Cultura e realizzata grazie al sostegno della Fondazione CRT, è dedicata all’artista nel centenario della sua nascita .

Le tre sedi offrono prospettive complementari sulla ricerca di Marisa Merz. Alla Fondazione Merz l’attenzione si concentra sui materiali, sui gesti e sui processi attraverso cui l’artista costruisce le proprie opere. Il percorso permette di avvicinarsi a una pratica fondata sulla sperimentazione, che attraversa materiali industriali e domestici, elementi poveri e soluzioni formali in continua evoluzione. Questa ricerca si sviluppa nel contesto torinese, in dialogo con la stagione dell’Arte Povera, conservando una propria autonomia rispetto alle sue definizioni e ai suoi confini.

Alla Fondazione Merz è esposta Arpa (1967–1968), opera in cui il filo metallico disegna una trama di linee, tensioni e aperture. La struttura appare leggera, sostenuta da un equilibrio preciso. Gli intervalli conferiscono autonomia ai singoli fili e ne rivelano le reciproche relazioni: ciascuno acquista intensità attraverso la distanza dagli altri. Il vuoto entra così nella composizione, rendendo percepibile l’interdipendenza delle linee. Una fotografia di Paolo Pellion documenta Marisa Merz durante l’installazione dell’opera a Torino nel 1973: il corpo dell’artista misura e organizza lo spazio, il gesto lascia nella trama la memoria di un’azione i cui effetti continuano a propagarsi oltre la propria conclusione.

Al Castello di Rivoli, la ricerca dell’artista assume una dimensione ambientale e spirituale. Il nucleo del percorso è la ricostruzione di E il naufragar m’è dolce in questo mare del 1980, ambiente presentato dall’artista alla galleria Tucci Russo di Torino e riproposto alla Biennale di Venezia nello stesso anno. Le opere di Merz sono inserite in un dialogo costante con quelle di dieci artiste contemporanee, dando vita a un confronto che attraversa l’intero allestimento e mette in relazione sensibilità, linguaggi e differenti modalità di intendere lo spazio. L’insieme dei lavori partecipa così alla costruzione di un percorso unitario, dove scultura, architettura e percezione si intrecciano.

Oltre sessanta lavori storici e recenti ampliano la riflessione sull’eredità e sull’attualità della ricerca dell’artista. In E il naufragar m’è dolce in questo mare lo spazio diventa parte integrante dell’opera. Gli elementi si dispongono secondo un equilibrio aperto, in cui pieno e vuoto si definiscono reciprocamente. L’ambiente coinvolge il corpo e lo sguardo, offrendo molteplici possibilità di osservazione. La dimensione spirituale affiora nell’esperienza diretta dello spazio, nella possibilità di attraversarlo e sostare davanti a forme che conservano una componente di mistero. Il vuoto si manifesta anche nelle relazioni tra le opere e tra queste e chi le osserva. La distanza diventa una condizione percettiva: permette alle forme di respirare e allo spettatore di costruire un proprio itinerario. Nel catalogo della mostra dedicata a Merz nel 1998, Rudi Fuchs sottolinea la capacità della sua ricerca di oltrepassare la consistenza materiale degli oggetti, coinvolgendo lo spazio e l’esperienza di chi guarda.

Alla GAM il progetto si concentra sul rapporto tra arte e vita, attraverso la casa intesa come luogo di lavoro, sperimentazione e trasformazione. La dimensione domestica ricorrente nella pratica di Marisa Merz costituisce uno spazio in cui quotidianità e creazione si incontrano. Oggetti, materiali e gesti ordinari diventano parte di una ricerca che estende il linguaggio artistico all’esperienza vissuta. In questo contesto si collocano anche le Living Sculpture (1966), opere appartenenti alla collezione della GAM la cui storia restituisce il carattere sperimentale e personale della pratica dell’artista. Il volto, ricorrente nelle opere pittoriche e scultoree, partecipa all’indagine sull’identità e sulla forma.

L’immagine conserva una natura instabile, attraversata da variazioni e trasformazioni, dove il riconoscimento convive con l’indeterminatezza. La figura umana rimane così aperta, sospesa tra apparizione e dissolvenza. Questa instabilità ne attraversa l’intera ricerca. Le opere si sottraggono a una configurazione definitiva: possono modificarsi, essere ricomposte, perdere o acquisire elementi. La materia diventa una realtà sensibile con cui Merz instaura un rapporto di ascolto e trasformazione. Nel testo You Can Make Shoes out of Brains , pubblicato nel catalogo The Sky Is a Great Space del 2017, Carolyn Christov-Bakargiev restituisce la singolarità di questa pratica, in cui l’immaginazione incontra la materia e trasforma gli elementi quotidiani in possibilità inattese. La danza delle ore restituisce la complessità di un’opera attraversata da molteplici dimensioni.

Le tre sedi ne evidenziano la capacità di intrecciare materiali, ambienti e forme dell’esperienza, raccontando una ricerca coerente e in continua evoluzione. Il vuoto diventa il principio che rende possibili le relazioni tra le forme, tra arte e vita, tra artista e spettatore. È uno spazio da attraversare, nel quale la forma continua a trasformarsi all’interno di un linguaggio autonomo e personale.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 在第61届威尼斯双年展上，塞内加尔艺术家卡罗琳·盖耶将纳瓦格罗宫（Palazzo Navagero）改造为一场对感知力的沉浸式探索，她利用黄金来质疑价值是如何被构建的，以及我们对世界的理解如何根据……

"几个世纪以来，黄金塑造了经济、政治权力和文化历史，然而它的价值与其说是理解它的信仰体系和感知密不可分，不如说是通过这些体系和感知被人们所理解。在第61届威尼斯双年展的塞内加尔馆中，卡罗琳·盖耶从一个意想不到的角度切入这一熟悉的材料。她的展览题为《WURUS》（在沃洛夫语中意为“黄金”），与其说它关乎贵金属本身，不如说它关乎决定我们看到什么、如何解读它以及我们认为什么是有价值的种种条件。卡罗琳·盖耶，《WURUS》，“结构场”细节。图片版权 "alt": "", "caption": "卡罗琳·盖耶，《WURUS》，“结构场”细节。图片版权 © 卡罗琳·盖耶。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由马桑巴·姆巴耶（Massamba Mbaye）策划的《WURUS》将这座历史建筑转变为一个沉浸式环境，其中建筑与雕塑融为一体。黑暗让位于意想不到的倒影，错综复杂的黄铜与青铜聚合物形态从隐蔽的空间中浮现，访客们穿梭于装置之中，他们所处的身体位置不断改变着哪些部分变得可见。凭借在基础物理学和天体物理学方面的背景，盖耶将空间视为一个活跃的关系系统，而非一件件物品的中性背景。在塞内加尔馆接受《ART "卡罗琳·盖耶：代表塞内加尔参加威尼斯双年展是一种荣誉，但这也是一份沉甸甸的责任。对于这次展览，我们选择了《WURUS》这个标题，它在沃洛夫语中意为“黄金”。黄金象征着欲望、权力、财富和历史，但我们希望从另一个不同的角度来切入：价值的问题。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "黄金是一种其价值看似不言而喻的材料，然而这种价值是通过我们与其关联的意义和系统构建出来的。在《WURUS》中，我们展示的并不是黄金本身。相反，我想创造一种体验，鼓励访客去质疑他们是如何感知某事物的，以及这种感知如何影响他们为其赋予的价值。卡罗琳·盖耶，《WURUS》，“碰撞后”细节。图片版权 © 卡罗琳·盖耶。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/CarolineGueye_WURUS_After-Collision_courtesy-of-the-artist_photo-Caroline-Gueye-773x1030.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "卡罗琳·盖耶，《WURUS》，“碰撞后”细节。图片版权 © 卡罗琳·盖耶。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你彻底改造了纳瓦格罗宫的内部。你是如何将建筑视为艺术品不可分割的一部分，而不仅仅是一个展示雕塑的空间的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们重建了整个展览空间，搭建墙壁并改变了房间的格局，因为我想让访客成为体验的一部分。根据你站立的位置以及你观看作品的方式，你的感知也会发生变化。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从一开始，我就将这座宫殿的改造本身构思为一件艺术品。墙壁、通道、开口和视角不仅仅是展览设计，也是艺术构图的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在历史建筑内部工作需要仔细的规划，并与当地制作团队紧密合作。我们必须将我的愿景转化为建筑图纸，同时尊重建筑的局限性。对我而言，展览并非放置在房间里的一组独立艺术品。一切都是相互联系的，空间和雕塑本身同样重要。卡罗琳·盖耶，《WURUS》，装置细节。图片版权 © 艾丽斯·萨托里（Alice Sartori）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/WhatsApp-Image-2026-10-12-at-10.05.34-773x1030.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "卡罗琳·盖耶，《WURUS》，装置细节。图片版权 © 艾丽斯·萨托里（Alice Sartori）。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "访客通过黑暗、倒影和意想不到的视角来邂逅你的雕塑。打破我们所看到的与我们自以为看到的事物之间的关系，有什么吸引你的地方？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当你进入展览时，你会发现自己身处一个光线非常微弱的相对黑暗的空间里。镜子和反射面随处可见，有时你会感到有点迷失。你会看到艺术品反射在不同的地方，而你并不总是确定自己看到的是一件物品还是它的倒影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我想创造这种体验是因为感知取决于某物变得可见的条件。有些雕塑会立即显现出来，而另一些则被部分隐藏，或者只有从特定的位置才能显露出来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "直接观察、从远处观察或通过倒影观察某物会产生不同的体验。这与价值问题息息相关，因为事物的呈现方式会影响我们对它的感知。卡罗琳·盖耶，《WURUS》，“‘结构场’元素”细节。图片版权 © 卡罗琳·盖耶。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/CarolineGueye_WURUS_Element-©-Courtesy-Caroline-Gueye-1030x773.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "卡罗琳·盖耶，《WURUS》，“‘结构场’元素”细节。图片版权 © 卡罗琳·盖耶。", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "运动对《WURUS》的体验至关重要。访客的身体位置如何影响哪些内容变得可见，这又揭示了感知与价值之间的什么关系？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在法语中，我们有一个词叫 parcours，用来描述一条路径或旅程。这就是我构思这个展览的方式。你必须穿行其中，因为你无法从单一的位置理解这个装置。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "参观者在展览中不再只是单纯的旁观者，而是成为了行动者。一件雕塑可能从一个角度清晰可见，从另一个角度消失，或者通过反射重新出现。运动改变了作品被感知的条件。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们往往认为我们所看到的是固定不变的，但它其实取决于我们的位置、距离和运动。我并不期望参观者得出某种单一的特定解释。重要的是，他们能体验到这种视角的转变，并意识到他们所看到的取决于他们所站立的位置。Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘Structural Field’Resonance’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/CarolineGueye_WURUS_Resonance-©-Courtesy-Caroline-Gueye-1030x773.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘Structural Field’Resonance’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你拥有基础物理学和天体物理学的背景，这如何塑造了你对空间及物体之间关系的理解？这种科学训练又是如何影响你的艺术思考以及 WURUS 的创作过程的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我认为我所受的基础物理学和天体物理学背景影响了我处理三维形态和空间的方式。这或许也可以解释为什么我的雕塑通常相当繁复且复杂。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的科学背景影响了我所提出的问题。例如在创作 WURUS 时，我开始对黄金的起源产生兴趣。在天体物理学中，黄金是由极端的宇宙事件（包括中子星碰撞）产生的。我也对它的科学与技术应用感兴趣，在这些领域中，它的电学、热学和光学特性尤为珍贵。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但科学并不是我想要去图解的东西。它是一种思考、质疑和理解关系的方式。对我而言，空间绝非仅仅是一个空容器，而是一个活跃的存在，由物体、形体和位置之间的关系所塑造。Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘Structural Field’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/CarolineGueye_WURUS_Structural-Field-©-Courtesy-Caroline-Gueye-1-773x1030.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘Structural Field’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你曾描述过一种不同寻常的创作过程：在制作图纸或模型之前，你就能在脑海中将整个装置可视化。这种过程是如何展开的？在将这些脑海中的构筑转化为实体形态时，又会遇到哪些挑战？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的创作过程非常特殊，因为我能在脑海中看到一切。它是如此清晰，以至于在展览问世之前，我就能想象自己在整个展览中穿行。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我发现这种能力或许并不寻常是在2022年的达喀尔双年展上，当时我的一个沉浸式装置作品获了奖。人们问我是如何创作出它的，我解释说我能在脑海中看到一切。通过那些对话，我意识到并不是每个人都这样工作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于 WURUS ，这个过程也是一样的。我可以想象出房间、雕塑、它们的位置以及参观者如何在空间中移动。我不一定需要图纸来理解某件作品应该呈现什么样子，尽管要把那种视觉构想转化为建筑图纸并向制作团队解释则是另一回事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于个别的雕塑来说，这个过程可能需要更多的实验，特别是在使用不熟悉的材料时。即使是尺寸或形态上的微小改变，也会影响作品被感知的方式。Caroline Gueye, WURUS , installation detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Opening-of-WURUS-by-Caroline-Gueye-—-Senegal-Pavillion-©-Loan-Montage-4-773x1030.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Caroline Gueye, WURUS , installation detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的雕塑是用黄铜和青铜聚合物制成的，这些材料在外观上酷似黄金，却不具备黄金的物质属性。这些选择，连同光线和反射表面，是如何共同促成你对被赋予的价值的探索的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我喜欢在创作时拥有自由，因为我所构想的形状通常很繁复且在技术上很有难度。我需要能够让我实现这些形态的材料。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了创作 WURUS ，我使用了黄铜和青铜聚合物，它们可以做得像黄金却并非真正的黄金。这种区分至关重要，因为这场展览探讨的正是不断变化的价值感知。当你看到某个看起来像是黄金的东西但它其实不是时，这就会引发关于外表如何影响我们对事物价值判断的思考。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "镜子、反射表面和灯光同样重要。它们不仅仅是营造氛围的元素，更是概念本身的一部分，它们影响着雕塑的呈现方式以及参观者的体验。这一切共同营造了一种不确定性，模糊了事物本身与我们感知到的事物之间的界限。Caroline Gueye and Massamba Mbaye. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Opening-of-WURUS-by-Caroline-Gueye-—-Senegal-Pavillion-©-Loan-Montage-3-773x1030.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Caroline Gueye and Massamba Mbaye. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在经济、文化和象征价值日益受到争议的时代， WURUS 就我们如何构建意义、赋予价值以及理解我们周围的世界提出了哪些更广泛的问题？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们正生活在一个价值变得越来越抽象、脱离物质性的时代。 WURUS 并没有直接将此作为一个议论的主题，而是创造了一种情境，让人们能够切身体验价值是如何被构建出来的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这场展览旨在改变我们感知事物的条件。物体本身并没有改变，但我们遭遇它们的方式改变了。它们的出现取决于我们的位置、运动、光线以及周围的空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我希望参观者能够成为装置的一部分，因为他们的存在促成了可见之物的诞生。从一个视角看显而易见的事物，换个角度可能会变得完全不同。我并不是要求人们得出某种特定的结论，而是希望他们体验到改变位置如何能够改变他们的感知。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
At the 61st Venice Biennale, Senegalese artist Caroline Gueye transforms Palazzo Navagero into an immersive exploration of perception, using gold to question how value is constructed and how our understanding of the world shifts depending on where we stand.

Gold has shaped economies, political power, and cultural histories for centuries, yet its value remains inseparable from the belief systems and perceptions through which we understand it. At the Senegal Pavilion of the 61st Venice Biennale, Caroline Gueye approaches this familiar material from an unexpected perspective. Her exhibition, WURUS , meaning ‘gold’ in Wolof, is less concerned with the precious metal itself than with the conditions that determine what we see, how we interpret it and what we consider valuable. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘Structural Field’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

Curated by Massamba Mbaye, WURUS transforms the historic building into an immersive environment where architecture and sculpture become inseparable. Darkness gives way to unexpected reflections, intricate brass-and-bronze polymer forms emerge from concealed spaces, and visitors navigate an installation in which their physical position continually alters what becomes visible. Drawing on her background in fundamental physics and astrophysics, Gueye approaches space as an active system of relationships rather than a neutral setting for objects. In conversation with ART AFRICA at the Senegal Pavilion, she reflects on representing her country, her unusual ability to visualise entire installations before they exist, and how movement, material, and perception can challenge established ideas of value.

ART AFRICA : Gold has long been associated with wealth, power and possession. What drew you to it as the starting point for WURUS, and how does the exhibition challenge our understanding of value?

Caroline Gueye: It is an honour to represent Senegal at the Venice Biennale, but it is also a big responsibility. For this exhibition, we chose the title WURUS , which means ‘gold’ in Wolof. Gold symbolises desire, power, wealth and history, but we wanted to approach it from a different perspective: the question of value.

Gold is a material whose value appears self-evident, yet that value is constructed through the meanings and systems we associate with it. In WURUS , we are not presenting gold itself. Instead, I wanted to create an experience that encourages visitors to question how they perceive something and how that perception influences the value they assign to it. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘After Collision’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

You have completely transformed the interior of Palazzo Navagero. How did you approach the architecture as an integral part of the artwork, rather than simply a space to exhibit sculptures?

We rebuilt the entire exhibition space, constructing walls and changing the room configuration because I wanted visitors to become part of the experience. Depending on where you stand and how you look at a work, your perception changes.

From the beginning, I conceived the transformation of the palazzo as an artwork in itself. The walls, passages, openings and viewpoints were not simply exhibition design but part of the artistic composition.

Working within a historic building required careful planning and collaboration with the local production team. We had to translate my vision into architectural drawings while respecting the building’s restrictions. For me, the exhibition is not a collection of separate artworks placed in a room. Everything is connected, and the space is as important as the sculptures themselves. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , Installation detail. Image © Alice Sartori.

Visitors encounter your sculptures through darkness, reflections and unexpected viewpoints. What interests you about disrupting the relationship between what we see and what we believe we are seeing?

When you enter the exhibition, you find yourself in a relatively dark space with very little light. Mirrors and reflective surfaces are everywhere, and sometimes you get a little lost. You see artworks reflected in different places, and you are not always certain whether you are looking at an object or its reflection.

I wanted to create this experience because perception depends on the conditions in which something becomes visible. Some sculptures appear immediately, while others are partially concealed or revealed only from particular positions.

Seeing something directly, from a distance or through a reflection produces different experiences. This connects to the question of value because how something appears influences how we perceive it. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , “Structural Field “Element’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

Movement is fundamental to the WURUS experience. How does the visitor’s physical position influence what becomes visible, and what does this reveal about the relationship between perception and value?

In French, we have the word parcours, which describes a path or journey. That is how I imagined this exhibition. You have to walk through it because you cannot understand the installation from a single position.

The visitor becomes an actor within the exhibition rather than simply an observer. A sculpture might be visible from one angle, disappear from another or reappear through a reflection. Movement changes the conditions in which the work is perceived.

We tend to think that what we see is fixed, but it depends on our position, distance and movement. I do not expect visitors to arrive at one particular interpretation. What matters is that they experience this shift and become aware that what they see depends on where they stand. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘Structural Field’Resonance’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

Your background in fundamental physics and astrophysics informs your understanding of space and the relationships between objects. How has this scientific training shaped your artistic thinking and the development of WURUS?

I think my background in fundamental physics and astrophysics shapes the way I work with three-dimensional forms and space. It may also explain why my sculptures are often quite intricate and complex.

My scientific background influences the questions I ask. With WURUS , for example, I became interested in where gold comes from. In astrophysics, gold is produced through extreme cosmic events, including neutron star collisions. I was also interested in its scientific and technological applications, where its electrical, thermal and optical properties are particularly valuable.

But science is not something I want to illustrate. It is a way of thinking, questioning and understanding relationships. For me, space is not simply an empty container but something active, shaped by the relationships between objects, bodies and positions. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘Structural Field’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

You have described an unusual creative process in which you can visualise an entire installation before producing drawings or models. How does this process unfold, and what challenges arise when translating these mental constructions into physical form?

My process is quite particular because I see everything in my head. It is so clear that I can walk through an entire exhibition in my imagination before it exists.

I discovered that this was perhaps unusual during the Dakar Biennale in 2022, where I received a prize for an immersive installation. People asked how I had created it, and I explained that I could see everything in my head. Through those conversations, I realised that not everybody works this way.

For WURUS , the process was the same. I could imagine the rooms, the sculptures, their positions and how visitors would move through the space. I do not necessarily need drawings to understand how something should look, although translating that vision into architectural plans and explaining it to the production team is another matter.

With individual sculptures, the process can require more experimentation, particularly when working with unfamiliar materials. Even a small change in scale or form can affect how a work is perceived. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , installation detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

Your sculptures are made from brass and bronze polymer, materials that resemble gold without possessing its material identity. How do these choices, together with light and reflective surfaces, contribute to your exploration of perceived value?

I like to have freedom when I create because the shapes I imagine are often intricate and technically difficult. I need materials that allow me to achieve those forms.

For WURUS , I used brass and bronze polymer, which can resemble gold without actually being gold. This distinction is important because the exhibition is about shifting perceptions of value. You look at something that appears to be gold, but it is not, which raises questions about how appearance influences what we think something is worth.

The mirrors, reflective surfaces and lighting are equally important. They are not simply atmospheric elements but part of the concept, influencing how the sculptures appear and how visitors experience them. Everything contributes to the uncertainty between what something is and what we perceive it to be. Caroline Gueye and Massamba Mbaye. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

At a time when economic, cultural, and symbolic values are increasingly contested, what broader questions does WURUS raise about how we construct meaning, assign value, and understand the world around us?

We are living in a moment when value is becoming increasingly abstract and detached from materiality. WURUS does not address this directly as a commentary, but it creates a situation in which people can experience how value is constructed.

The exhibition is about changing the conditions through which we perceive something. The objects themselves do not necessarily change, but the way we encounter them does. Their appearance depends on our position, movement, the light and the surrounding space.

I wanted visitors to become part of the installation because their presence contributes to what becomes visible. Something that appears obvious from one perspective may become quite different from another. I am not asking people to arrive at a particular conclusion, but to experience how changing their position can change their perception.

title_original: Restoring the fractured archive: SWANA collective memory at BredaPhoto Festival
editorial_title_zh: 修复破碎的档案：布雷达摄影节上的 SWANA 集体记忆
editorial_excerpt_zh: 作为更广泛的布雷达摄影节的一部分，来自 SWANA 地区的艺术家们带来了一系列展览，他们打破了单一的媒体驱动叙事，呈现出更丰富、更细腻的视角。

true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈拉克对旧时照相馆肖像画充满着迷，并为其因战争而消逝感到痛心，于是他在大马士革的街头搭建了一个临时的移动摄影棚。通过邀请当地居民拍摄肖像，他用自己的系列作品《大马士革照相馆》（Studio Damascus）构建了叙利亚存在状况的新档案。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“当生存成为日常生活的一部分时，拍一张肖像这样简单的举动也变得困难重重，”他说道。“我相信，和家人拍张肖像可以成为一种稳定的象征。当我指导镜头前的人们时，这种连结创造了一个让他们能够暂时脱离不稳定状态的时刻。《大马士革照相馆》探讨了重聚、记忆、归属感，以及人类对稳定的需求。”哈拉克拒绝将一个正艰难应对破碎国家的社群的现实扁平化。“在经历了这一切之后，我仍然觉得人们有一种渴望，想要把这些现实变得更容易理解，”他总结道。“我不认为问题在于误解。这正是我在实践中所追寻的——一种源自人类情感的语言。某种感性的、亲密的，甚至可能是精神层面的东西。”", "British Journal of Photography", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与此同时，摄影师兼电影人法蒂玛·朱马（Fatima Lebanon）中，她将影像穿插在她母亲莱拉（Layla）旧时的笔记与草图之间，创作出一部关于悲伤、记忆以及作为历史守护者的女性的沉思录。朱马将纪实摄影、诗意的视频散文以及第一手的当地证词结合起来，直接挑战了通常对战争的媒体表现形式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "每当黎巴嫩的生活遭到破坏——而且仅在过去七年中，在以色列对南部的当前种族灭绝式袭击和占领发生很久之前，就已经发生了许多复合危机——全球的影像创作者便会蜂拥至街头，捕捉瞬时的暴力与瓦砾、悲伤与愤怒，随后又同样迅速地离去。这种高速的纪实报道留下了朱马所称的“后像”（after-image），她将这一概念发展成了为黎巴嫩独立杂志《公众之源》（The Public Source）撰写的一个系列文章。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她将目光转向那些安静的、缓慢燃烧的余波，以及在侵入性的摄像机离开后展现出的复杂内在性，以此对抗那些将整个社区及其居民贬低为被动荒凉之地的顽固陈词滥调。“我一直意识到，无论是动态影像还是静态影像，图像被当作一种可提取的资源对待的程度有多高，”她说道。“通常情况下，当国际媒体或机构接触我们时，他们想要图像是因为它带有一种真实性——但他们希望由自己来决定这种真实性被允许包含什么内容。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我曾被要求移除旗帜、烈士肖像、政治标语，或是任何可能让图像在他们看来显得过于政治化的东西，就好像有什么东西不是政治的一样，”她继续说道。“而我拒绝仅仅把我的同胞描绘成受害者。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Held within the wider BredaPhoto Festival, a strand of exhibitions by artists from the SWANA region dismantles flat media-driven narratives to present richer, more nuanced perspectives"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For decades, the visual vocabulary assigned to the Southwest Asia and North Africa (SWANA) region by the international world of photography has been an exercise in transactional observation. A hyper-visible taxonomy of ruin, anchored in flattened and anonymised rage and grief, manufactures a state of perpetual exception, flattening complex social topographies into spectacles that court Western pity while burying structural truth. Within global institutions, regional image-makers are mined for local authenticity but systematically stripped of political urgency; international editors sanitise symbols of local resistance to satisfy detached audiences, while treating practitioners’ lived experiences as barely compensated raw material."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yet a slow but steady shift in lens-based practices is gaining momentum, even in traditional and so-called apolitical spaces. Rather than seeking to correct the distorted mirrors held up by so many foreign photographers, or bending to the restrictive mandates of international gatekeepers, an emerging generation of image-makers, researchers, and storytellers is choosing to bypass these institutions, or only engage with them on their own terms. They are constructing what can be termed a “counter-archive”, not as a nostalgic retreat into a static past, but as an intentional, self-authored historical record of perpetual survival towards ultimate liberation."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This critical reclamation underpins a strand of the exhibitions in the current BredaPhoto Festival, which is themed Our Songs Came Through . Co-curated by Mohamed Somji, Ileana L. Selejan, and Astrid Hulsmann, the biennial explores how individuals and communities find solace and comfort (or “troost” in Dutch) and how intimate imagery and memory can puncture institutional erasure. These questions are key in the SWANA context."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/abdulmughni02.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Huda Abdulmughni's work on show at BredaPhoto Festival", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "quote", "text": "“ This kind of work gives us the tools to crack open a radical collective imagination.” Noor Abed"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Somji’s curatorial approach is characterised by a rigorous push towards self-authored storytelling, honed through his experience programming at Gulf Photo Plus, including at its popular Slidefest evenings. There developing regional practitioners are given the space to express their grievances and interrogate their motivations, away from the Western gaze. Inherited hierarchies of recognition are consistently broken down. But manifesting this dialogue in an exhibition in a Western institution can be challenging."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“When we started talking about this theme toward the end of the last festival, I was skeptical about how easily it could become very kumbaya – a superficial ‘let’s all go into the mountains, cleanse our world, and come back’ approach, while mass killing and active displacement are unfolding in Palestine, Lebanon, Yemen, Sudan, Iran and elsewhere,” says Somji. “We went back and forth on the texts and the selections of artists, work, and more, to make sure the structural, political reality was firmly addressed."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Through GPP, we’ve spent years building an infrastructure for self-authored stories, because we know the damage of institutional erasure,” he continues. “The artists featured here aren’t just capturing conflict, they are archiving the poetry, the domestic resistance, and the psychological architectures that endure when people insist on surviving on their own terms.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Also-Video-Still-Noor-Abed-2.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Video still © Noor Abed", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/This-NoorAbed_00_18_41_06.Still024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Video still © Noor Abed", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Palestinian artist Noor Abed’s specially-commissioned video installation, we walk in our sleep , presents a poetic blueprint of Palestinian realities, for example, subverting the clinical approaches of mainstream media and military occupation. Outsiders’ depictions of Palestine have often relied on the iconography of the barrier – checkpoints, watchtowers, concrete walls, and actively-restricted freedom. This centres the occupier’s gaze, defining Palestinian life entirely by that which restricts it. Abed adamantly refuses this framework."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Working in close collaboration with her family and neighbours, she turns the lens inward to examine how land is claimed, remembered, and mythologised through collective, physical ritual. we walk in our sleep moves through a series of vignettes, showing people whose gestures hover between ancient agrarian labor and contemporary performance art. Synchronised figures moving across open hillsides, the subtle positions of their heads and hands invoke histories that predate violent colonial sketches. Projected in a completely darkened, small room with only a tiny bench to sit on, the film is difficult to categorise; it’s overwhelming, in a way that feels necessary."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Abed was initially inspired to make the film when she noticed people muttering to themselves on the streets of her hometown; after many sleepless nights of contemplation, she connected this phenomenon to something else she had already zoned in on, the sacred space between the living and the dead. Abed believes that the martyrs walk among us."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“For many, many years now, I’ve been contemplating the wide range of rituals around mourning and death, which is something we witness every day,” Abed explains. “In the last few years, it started to become physical. The dead are among us, I truly believe that. So for me, it’s almost like carving into this space, the air around me. It became an exercise of listening to and being close to the martyrs [those who have been unjustly killed].”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Video-Still-Noor-Abed-1.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Video still © Noor Abed", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Abed’s work maps a psychological landscape that remains inaccessible to the colonial apparatus; a checkpoint can bisect a road, but it cannot erase the collective memory of a community that has walked, sung, and lived on that land for thousands of years.
