article_text:
Held within the wider BredaPhoto Festival, a strand of exhibitions by artists from the SWANA region dismantles flat media-driven narratives to present richer, more nuanced perspectives

For decades, the visual vocabulary assigned to the Southwest Asia and North Africa (SWANA) region by the international world of photography has been an exercise in transactional observation. A hyper-visible taxonomy of ruin, anchored in flattened and anonymised rage and grief, manufactures a state of perpetual exception, flattening complex social topographies into spectacles that court Western pity while burying structural truth. Within global institutions, regional image-makers are mined for local authenticity but systematically stripped of political urgency; international editors sanitise symbols of local resistance to satisfy detached audiences, while treating practitioners’ lived experiences as barely compensated raw material.

Yet a slow but steady shift in lens-based practices is gaining momentum, even in traditional and so-called apolitical spaces. Rather than seeking to correct the distorted mirrors held up by so many foreign photographers, or bending to the restrictive mandates of international gatekeepers, an emerging generation of image-makers, researchers, and storytellers is choosing to bypass these institutions, or only engage with them on their own terms. They are constructing what can be termed a “counter-archive”, not as a nostalgic retreat into a static past, but as an intentional, self-authored historical record of perpetual survival towards ultimate liberation.

This critical reclamation underpins a strand of the exhibitions in the current BredaPhoto Festival, which is themed Our Songs Came Through . Co-curated by Mohamed Somji, Ileana L. Selejan, and Astrid Hulsmann, the biennial explores how individuals and communities find solace and comfort (or “troost” in Dutch) and how intimate imagery and memory can puncture institutional erasure. These questions are key in the SWANA context.

“ This kind of work gives us the tools to crack open a radical collective imagination.” Noor Abed

Somji’s curatorial approach is characterised by a rigorous push towards self-authored storytelling, honed through his experience programming at Gulf Photo Plus, including at its popular Slidefest evenings. There developing regional practitioners are given the space to express their grievances and interrogate their motivations, away from the Western gaze. Inherited hierarchies of recognition are consistently broken down. But manifesting this dialogue in an exhibition in a Western institution can be challenging.

“When we started talking about this theme toward the end of the last festival, I was skeptical about how easily it could become very kumbaya – a superficial ‘let’s all go into the mountains, cleanse our world, and come back’ approach, while mass killing and active displacement are unfolding in Palestine, Lebanon, Yemen, Sudan, Iran and elsewhere,” says Somji. “We went back and forth on the texts and the selections of artists, work, and more, to make sure the structural, political reality was firmly addressed.

“Through GPP, we’ve spent years building an infrastructure for self-authored stories, because we know the damage of institutional erasure,” he continues. “The artists featured here aren’t just capturing conflict, they are archiving the poetry, the domestic resistance, and the psychological architectures that endure when people insist on surviving on their own terms.”

Palestinian artist Noor Abed’s specially-commissioned video installation, we walk in our sleep , presents a poetic blueprint of Palestinian realities, for example, subverting the clinical approaches of mainstream media and military occupation. Outsiders’ depictions of Palestine have often relied on the iconography of the barrier – checkpoints, watchtowers, concrete walls, and actively-restricted freedom. This centres the occupier’s gaze, defining Palestinian life entirely by that which restricts it. Abed adamantly refuses this framework.

Working in close collaboration with her family and neighbours, she turns the lens inward to examine how land is claimed, remembered, and mythologised through collective, physical ritual. we walk in our sleep moves through a series of vignettes, showing people whose gestures hover between ancient agrarian labor and contemporary performance art. Synchronised figures moving across open hillsides, the subtle positions of their heads and hands invoke histories that predate violent colonial sketches. Projected in a completely darkened, small room with only a tiny bench to sit on, the film is difficult to categorise; it’s overwhelming, in a way that feels necessary.

Abed was initially inspired to make the film when she noticed people muttering to themselves on the streets of her hometown; after many sleepless nights of contemplation, she connected this phenomenon to something else she had already zoned in on, the sacred space between the living and the dead. Abed believes that the martyrs walk among us.

“For many, many years now, I’ve been contemplating the wide range of rituals around mourning and death, which is something we witness every day,” Abed explains. “In the last few years, it started to become physical. The dead are among us, I truly believe that. So for me, it’s almost like carving into this space, the air around me. It became an exercise of listening to and being close to the martyrs [those who have been unjustly killed].”

Abed’s work maps a psychological landscape that remains inaccessible to the colonial apparatus; a checkpoint can bisect a road, but it cannot erase the collective memory of a community that has walked, sung, and lived on that land for thousands of years. She refuses to use folklore as mere nostalgia, but positions it as a perpetual tool of survival, demonstrating its inherent political utility. Her lens is patient and meditative, a direct rejection of the high-velocity aesthetic of breaking news stories disseminated in a 24-hour cycle; instead it asserts an invisible, unbreakable network of spatial permanence.

“For me, it’s a work of deliberate digging, of continuous searching – instead of considering the past as framed and fixed,” she says. “Because this is very dangerous, particularly in the context of Palestine. Once the past is turned into mere symbols, there is a risk of not being able to breathe anymore. It becomes empty. And for me, the collective memory is all about the embodied practices, knowledge, our rituals and the visceral connection to our land – whether in joy or in loss, in a funeral for a martyr that turns into celebration.”

Abed insists on the preservation of memories, by transforming them and keeping them connected to the present. “To simply lean on the past in this utopian way, with distance, there is no resistance for that in me,” she says. “This kind of work gives us the tools to crack open a radical collective imagination, that gives us both the hope and the means to rehearse liberation. Because there is no future other than liberation.”

While Abed maps the deep roots of connection to the land, Fouad Hallak’s A Mind in the Past, Eyes on Tomorrow addresses the fractured geometries of exile and return. Born in Syria, Hallak fled the country on a migrant vessel to claim asylum in the Netherlands; his work shifts away from diasporic trauma towards an internalised psychogeography. His recent documentation tracks his return to his homeland, in transition following the fall of Assad, capturing the fragile space between historical devastation and actualised hope.

“After the fall of the Assad regime, I noticed that people often looked at what happened in two different ways – some stories were bright, and others were painful,” Hallak reflects. “But these feelings can exist at the same time. When I went back, I was not an outsider. I was part of the story. I see this in the photograph of Khaled, who protested and fought against the regime. He carries his history with him and still moves forward… Before, this possibility did not exist. Now it does. For me, that is hope.”

Fascinated by old studio portraiture, and saddened by its disappearance due to war, Hallak created a temporary mobile setup in the streets of Damascus. Inviting residents to have their portraits taken, he constructed a new archive of Syrian presence with his series, Studio Damascus.

“When survival becomes part of everyday life, the simple act of having a portrait taken becomes difficult,” he says. “I believe that having a portrait taken with your family can be a sign of stability. When I direct people in front of the camera, the connection creates a moment in which they can step away from their instability. Studio Damascus explores reunion, memory, belonging, and the human need for stability.” Hallak refuses to flatten the reality of a community navigating a shattered state. “After all these years, I still feel there is a desire to make these realities easier to understand,” he concludes. “I don’t think the problem is misunderstanding. This is what I search for in my practice – a language that comes from human feeling. Something emotional, intimate, and perhaps even spiritual.”

Meanwhile photographer and filmmaker Fatima Joumaa turns the counter-archive towards the structural realities of South Lebanon (Al-Janoub) and Beirut’s southern suburbs (Dahiyeh). In her intimate project From My Mother’s Novel: Returning to South Lebanon , she weaves images through her mother Layla’s old notes and sketches, creating a meditation on grief, memory, and women as keepers of history. Joumaa combines analogue photography, poetic video essays, and first-hand local testimonies to directly challenge the usual media representations of war.

Whenever life in Lebanon is ruptured – and there have been many compounding crises over the past seven years alone, long before Israel’s current genocidal assault and occupation of the South – global image-makers flood the streets, capturing the immediate violence and debris, the grief and rage, before equally swiftly departing. This high-velocity reportage leaves what Joumaa calls an “after-image” in its wake, a concept she has developed into a series for independent Lebanese magazine The Public Source .

Shifting her gaze toward the quiet, slow-burning aftermath and complex interiorities that unfold after the intrusive cameras leave, she fights the persistent clichés that reduce entire neighbourhoods and their inhabitants to passive sites of devastation. “I was always aware of how much the image is treated as an extractable resource, whether moving or still,” she says. “And often, when international media or institutions approach us, they want the image because it carries a kind of authenticity – but they want to decide what that authenticity is allowed to contain.

“I have been asked to remove flags, portraits of martyrs, political signs, or anything that might make the image appear too political to them, as if there’s anything that isn’t political,” she continues. “And I refuse to portray my people only as victims.”

Joumaa argues these signifiers are at the core of this landscape, not mere additions to it – and that removing them does not render the image more neutral. Quite the opposite. “It produces another complete image, one that is more comfortable for the institution,” she says. “To them, it simply checks a box of exclusivity [paying lip-service to local perspectives] rather than talking about what is fundamentally happening.”

For Joumaa, the Israeli assault on South Lebanon, and its systematic violent occupation and genocidal destruction of almost all of the land in the region, is an everyday reality. She could not return to her village in Janoub to bury her grandmother, as is the reality for many families in South Lebanon. But by integrating first-person local testimonies into her video essays, she ensures that the voices of the community dictate the narrative arc of the work; the record of survival is written in the smallest, most intimate – most often overlooked – pockets of human existence.

Centring the camera on home-bound networks of care, Joumaa suggests that sovereignty is maintained through everyday acts of defiance, not on a grand geopolitical stage. And her insistence on documenting the unseen, foundational rhythms of community forms a natural bridge to Kuwaiti photographer and researcher Huda Abdulmughni, whose work focuses on the ancestral landscape.

Where Joumaa’s lens operates as an almost forensic instrument within the targeted spaces of her land and people, Abdulmughni focuses on a different kind of survival – one grounded in ecological harmony and collective memory. Abdulmughni’s Nowruz Sayadeen documents the annual fisherman’s New Year on the Iranian island of Qeshm, for example, in which the village’s primary source of income is paused, out of respect for nature’s seasonal bounty. Using both analogue and digital media, Abdulmughni captures the highly-stylised, almost mythical cast of characters populating the shores, including the iconic shushis – figures adorned with white face paint and palm leaves.

But rather than presenting the figures as exotic subjects, performing in costume once a year, Abdulmughni captures a world that relies on ancestral knowledge of the seas. Depicting traditions passed down through the generations, outside the strict categories preferred by Western ethnography, Abdulmughni’s work demonstrates that regional sovereignty is preserved through seasonal rhythms and ancestral ecological care. But her work also shows that this is also a world increasingly impacted by climate change due to geopolitical conflict, in which the community’s harmony with the earth may be devastated.

The biennial takes a devastating turn to remind us of the stakes raised when gentle rhythms are severed by colonial violence, including a posthumous show by Majd Arandas, A Memorial in Fragments . Arandas’ work brings the viewer face-to-face with the realities of active elimination; born in Gaza in 1994, he was killed in an Israeli airstrike near his home in Deir al-Balah on 01 November 2023. Arandas had long ago been forced to sell his professional camera to survive the Israeli blockade, but continued to document with his mobile phone, and his archive has been retrieved and preserved by his brother.

Somji wanted to honour Arandas’ work and life, but also show the networks of solidarity that surrounded him, and now surround his archive. “Whether it’s a beautiful exchange between Majd and a friend about the plants in his beloved grandmother’s garden, or a photographer friend exchanging cat photos with him, it shows how communities find ways to bond together, and provide solace, despite everything that’s against them, despite the challenges of neoliberal worlds and neo-colonialist regimes,” Somji says.

Arandas’ surviving images testify to what it means to create an archive when your existence is being contested in real-time. But he photographed Gaza with luminous tenderness, his images capturing quiet gestures of affection, subtle exchanges of care, and the warm, amber lights of temporary shelters. His work refuses to let his people be remembered solely by their erasure, insisting instead on the profound beauty and unyielding right to exist that defined their daily survival.

These exhibitions help make Our Songs Came Through a significant biennale; they also surface the often behind-the-scenes negotiations required to present these images within a Western framework. Organising exhibitions of work by independent SWANA practitioners in a European institution is a change, even in an institution known for pushing the envelope; more than that, it is a linguistic, bureaucratic, and geopolitical battleground. A violent manifestation of this gatekeeping is the European Visa system, for example, which prevented Libyan artist Amera Elnaal from entering the Netherlands to attend her own exhibition.

Our Songs Came Through is an intervention in the contemporary photography landscape, gathering an eclectic group of somehow connected artists to move far beyond the tokenism that often plagues Western institutions’ attempts to showcase art from the SWANA region. Rather than grouping these artists under a banner of shared trauma, it highlights their shared commitment to visual sovereignty, formal experimentation, and archival repair. The artists gathered here demonstrate that, to restore a fractured archive, one cannot simply add more images. Rather, we must fundamentally reinvent the methodology of image-making.

Collectively, the SWANA artists exhibiting at BredaPhoto are dismantling the familiar, flat, media-driven narratives. They remind us that history is not merely written by the victors, even those who wield a camera; it is unobtrusively and persistently preserved in the songs that survive, the rituals that map, and the communities which refuse to be forgotten. The fractured archive is reimagined as a site of radical agency, resistance, and complexity, and it honours the nuances of daily human survival.

BredaPhoto Festival 2026, Our Songs Came Through, is open until 25 October https://bredaphoto.nl

Farah-Silvana Kanaan is a Lebanese-Italian-Dutch writer, editor and creative consultant based between Amsterdam and Beirut. Her words have appeared in Kinfolk, Dazed, Rolling Stone, Discontent, Middle East Eye, and elsewhere.

Photography", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "巴勒斯坦艺术家诺尔·阿贝德的专门委托的视频安装,我们在睡眠中走路,展示了巴勒斯坦现实的诗意图,例如,扭曲了主要媒体和军事占领的临床方法。阿比德强烈拒绝了这个框架。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与家人和邻居密切合作,她转向镜头,以探讨土地是如何被声称,记住,并通过集体,物理仪式神话化。我们走在我们的睡眠中移动一系列的葡萄酒,展示的人,其动作在古老的农业劳动和当代表演艺术之间旋转。一个小房间,只有一个小床上坐着,电影很难分类;它是夸张的,以一种感觉需要的方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿贝德最初被激励拍摄这部电影,当她注意到人们在她故乡的街道上自欺欺;经过许多无眠的夜晚的观察,她将这个现象与她已经在某种东西联系起来,即活人与死人之间的神圣空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“多年来,现在,我一直在观察周围的各种仪式,痛苦和死亡,这是我们每天见证的东西,”阿贝德解释道,“过去几年,它开始变得物理,死者在我们中间,我真的相信,所以对我来说,它几乎像在这个空间,空气周围,它变成一个练习,倾听和接近烈士(那些不公平地被杀害的人)。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Video-Still-Noor-Abed-1.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "影片名稱:Noor Abed", "credit": "British Journal of Photography", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿贝德的工作地图描绘了一个心理景观,它仍然无法进入殖民装置;一个检查点可以打破一条路,但它不能消除一个社区的集体记忆,它已经在该土地上行走,唱歌,生活了数千年。在24小时周期中传播的破坏新闻故事的美学;相反,它声称一个不可见的,不可破坏的空间永久性网络。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“对于我来说,这是故意挖掘,不断寻找,而不是把过去看作是框架和固定的,”她说,“因为这很危险,尤其是在巴勒斯坦的背景下,一旦过去变成简单的象征,就有可能不再能呼吸,它变得空虚。失去,在一个为一个烈士的葬礼上,变成一个庆祝活动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿贝德坚持保持记忆,通过转变它们,并将它们与现在保持联系,“以这种乌托邦的方式,与距离,只是在过去,没有抵抗,在我内心,”她说,“这种工作给了我们工具,以打破一个激进的集体想象力,这给了我们希望和手段,以恢复解放,因为没有别的未来,除了解放。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "paragraph", "text": "虽然阿贝德地图了与土地的深根连接,福亚德·哈拉克的过去的思想,明天的眼睛处理了流离失所和回归的分裂地质。出生在叙利亚,哈拉克在移民船上逃离了该国,要求在荷兰的庇护;他的作品从分裂的创伤转向一个内在化的心理地理。历史的破坏和更新的希望。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“在阿萨德政权崩溃后,我注意到人们经常以两种不同的方式观察发生的事情 - 有些故事是明亮的,而其他故事是痛苦的,”哈拉克反思,“但是这些感觉可以同时存在,当我回来时,我不是一个外星人,我是故事的一部分,我看到这一点在哈雷德的照片中,他抗议并与政权作斗争,他携带他的历史,他仍然在前进......以前,这种可能性没有存在,现在,对我来说,这是希望。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈拉克因战争而失踪而感到震惊,在大马士革的街道上创建了一个暂时的移动设置,邀请居民拍摄他们的肖像,他与他的系列《大马士革工作室》建立了一个新的叙利亚存在档案。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“当生存成为日常生活的一部分时,一个肖像的简单行为变得困难,”他说,“我相信与家人一起拍摄肖像可以成为稳定的迹象,当我向摄像机前的人指导时,连接创造了一个时刻,他们可以从不稳定中脱颖而出。“我觉得有欲望让这些现实更容易理解,”他结论,“我不认为问题是误解,这是我在实践中寻找的,一种来自人类感受的语言,一些情感,亲密,也许甚至精神的东西。", "translated": true}, "她把她的焦虑转向沉默的,缓慢燃烧的后果和复杂的内心,在侵入摄像机离开后爆发,她打击了持续的幻灯片,将整个邻居和他们的居民减少到被动的破坏场所,“我一直意识到图像是如何被视为一个可取消的资源,无论是移动还是继续,”她说。这些真实性可以包含什么。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我被要求删除旗帜、烈士肖像、政治标志或任何可能让图像看起来太政治,就好像有什么不政治的东西,”她继续说,“我拒绝仅仅描绘我的民众为受害者。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/This-FatimaJomaa_FromMyMothersNovel_03.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "《我母亲的小说》(Fatima Joumaa)", "credit": "British Journal of Photography", Photography", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在朱马达的镜头在其土地和人民的目标空间内作为一个几乎法学工具,阿卜杜勒穆恩尼专注于一种不同的生存方式 - 一个基于生态和集体记忆的根源。阿卜杜勒穆恩尼的诺布鲁兹·萨伊登纪录每年渔民的新年在伊朗岛的Qeshm,例如,在那里村庄的主要收入来源休息,不尊重自然的季节性财富。捕捉了海岸人口的人物,其中包括标志性的沙希斯 - 与白色面部涂料和棕<unk>叶装饰的人物的高度风格,几乎神话般的组合。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但是,而不是把数字作为异国情调的主体,每年一次穿上衣服,阿卜杜勒穆尼捕捉着一个依赖于祖先的海洋知识的世界。 描绘传统经过几代,除了西方民族学所偏好的严格类别之外,阿卜杜勒穆尼的作品表明,区域主权是通过季节性节奏和祖先的生态护理保存的。地缘政治冲突,在那里社区与地球的和谐可能会被破坏。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿兰达斯的生存图像证明了在实时争论你的存在时创建一个档案的意义,但他以光明的温柔拍摄了加沙,他的图像捕获了安静的爱情动作,微妙的照顾交换,以及临时避难所的温暖和温暖的灯光。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些展览有助于通过一个显著的双年;它们也表面了经常背后的场景谈判需要在一个西方框架内展示这些图像。组织由独立的SWANA实习生在一个欧洲机构的工作展览是一个变化,即使在一个机构被称为推动包围;更多,它是一个语言,官僚和地缘政治战场。利比亚艺术家阿米拉·埃尔纳尔(Amerah Elnaal)从荷兰进入参加自己的展览。", excerpt_original: Held within the wider BredaPhoto Festival, a strand of exhibitions by artists from the SWANA region dismantles flat media-driven narratives to present richer, more nuanced perspectives
translated_title_zh: 恢复破碎的档案:SWANA在BredaPhoto Festival的集体记忆
translated_excerpt_zh: 在更广泛的BredaPhoto节内,SWANA地区艺术家展览的广场解散了平面媒体导向的故事,展示了更丰富、更色调的视野。

article_text:
Contents

1 Going out: Cinema

2 Going out: Gigs

3 Going out: Art

4 Going out: Stage

5 Staying in: Streaming

6 Staying in: Games

7 Staying in: Albums

8 Staying in: Brain food

Going out: Cinema

Wicker Out now Anyone who has ever fantasised about having a husband made out of wicker (surely a universal dream) will want to get themselves along to this Olivia Colman romantasy about a loner fisher who does exactly that. With Alexander Skarsgård, Richard E Grant, Peter Dinklage and Elizabeth Debicki.

Nightborn Out now Seidi Haarla gives a wonderfully unhinged performance as a woman convinced there is something wrong with her newborn baby: the hellish crying, her bleeding nipples … surely this child is a monster? All will be revealed in this tense but humorous supernatural drama, with Rupert Grint having fun as the sceptical new father.

Primetime Out now Robert Pattinson continues a recent hot streak with a characterful turn as Chris Hansen, the TV personality famous for fronting To Catch a Predator, the US hit that lured and publicly exposed men who were interested in having sex with teenagers. Directed by Lance Oppenheim (also on a hot streak with You Can See Everything).

I Love Boosters Out now Shoplifting, teleportation, the consequences of sweatshop labour, designer fashion, workers’ rights and demons who suck out your soul while performing oral sex: here’s a comedy from Boots Riley that has it all. Keke Palmer, Naomi Ackie and Taylour Paige star as Bay Area shoplifters the Velvet Gang, with Demi Moore as a powerful designer. Catherine Bray

Going out: Gigs

Pitchfork music festival London Various venues, 2 to 9 November The always divisive music website returns with another city festival lineup featuring the best in alternative soundscapes. Highlights include the Avalanches, Olof Dreijer, Jacob Alon and Keiyaa, plus Nigel Godrich’s new project Dragonflies, while the best band name goes to Psychedelic Porn Crumpets. Michael Cragg

Papa Roach 1 to 9 November; tour starts Glasgow Twenty-six years after their breakthrough with second album Infest, the perpetually angry nu-metallers are still going strong. Expect a heavy focus on that album – Last Resort is pretty undeniable in a live scenario – and follow-up Lovehatetragedy on this huge arena tour. MC

Guildhall School’s Opera Double Bill Silk Street theatre, London, 2 to 9 November Students on one of the country’s leading conservatoire opera courses perform two mid-century works: the UK premiere of Gian Carlo Menotti’s comic one-acter Amelia Al Ballo and Bernstein’s jazz-soaked modern classic Trouble in Tahiti. Expect high-energy professionalism and a chance to pick out the opera stars of the future. Flora Willson

Fergus McCreadie The Glasshouse, Sage Two, Gateshead, 5 November Since 2021, young pianist/composer Fergus McCreadie has grown in stature within the restless evolution of contemporary global jazz as a Mercury prize nominee, the traditional folk music of his Scottish homeland, and at the cutting edge of chamber music. The Glasshouse’s Innovators programme and Chamber Music Scotland showcase this adventurous wildlife-inspired co‑commission. John Fordham

Going out: Art

Winston Taylor Photo Portrait prize National Portrait Gallery, London, 5 November to 17 January The biggest photographic portraiture prize in the country has rebranded – you might know it better as the Taylor Wessing – but is otherwise unchanged: expect the finest photography by established pros and amateurs alike, featuring work from James Clifford Kent’s long-term project Yuma, including his portrait of aspiring pentathlete Neisser Yoel Gálvez Tabares.

Mad Bloomsbury Charleston Firle, Lewes, 4 November to 11 April Coinciding with the centenary of Virginia Woolf’s essay On Being Ill, this show looks at how the Bloomsbury Group – the likes of Roger Fry, Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant – dealt with ideas of madness, disability and neurodiversity.

Steve McQueen: Resistance Leeds Art Gallery , 6 November to 25 April Deeply moving documentation of how acts of resistance and rebellion have transformed the UK, all conceived by the brilliant Turner prize-winning artist and Oscar-winning director Steve McQueen.

The Nue Black Aesthetic Design Museum, London, 6 November to 8 August This display of more than 100 objects celebrates the black creatives who are shaping the future of design in Britain, including Taiba Akhuetie, Ini Archibong and Tejumola Adenuga. Eddy Frankel

Going out: Stage

Jordan Brookes Touring to 27 November; starts Bristol In 2019, the Surrey-raised standup expressed his long-held ambition to become “the existential Michael McIntyre”. In his excellent new show, The Part of You That’s Always Screaming, Brookes reaches those heights, with an unlikely combination of laugh-out-loud observational comedy and genuinely terrifying evocations of the abyss. Rachel Aroesti

Peanut Butter and Blueberries Leeds Playhouse, to 7 November After opening to strong reviews at Kiln theatre, Suhaiymah Manzoor-Khan’s thoughtful romcom transfers to Leeds. It’s about two university students and practising Muslims who move to London from the north, fall in love – but come up against harsh realities and rumbling racism. Miriam Gillinson

Hamlet Hail to the Thief Barbican theatre, London, to 23 January Steven Hoggett and Christine Jones’s music- and movement-infused Hamlet lands in London. The backbone of the show is Radiohead’s 2003 album Hail to the Thief, which frontman Thom Yorke has stripped back, rewired and threaded through the show with electrifying intent. MG

Luail: Nōs The Mac, Belfast, to 7 November Only formed two years ago, Luail is Ireland’s all-island national dance company, spanning Northern Ireland and the Republic. Their triple bill includes works by Belfast’s own Oona Doherty, Liz Roche and a classic from Akram Khan. Lyndsey Winship

after newsletter promotion

Staying in: Streaming

Yaga Sky Atlantic, 31 October , 9pm Hudson Williams swaps romance for folklore fantasy as he follows his star-making turn in Heated Rivalry by playing two characters – the missing scion of a wealthy family and his odd housemate – in Kat Sandler’s adaptation of her own play. Could a witchy professor be the key to it all?

The Rise of the Rockstar Chef BBC Two/iPlayer, 5 November , 9pm The collective yearning for 2000s monoculture continues to be stoked with this documentary series about three of the decade’s rule-breaking, gamechanging chefs: Marco Pierre White, Heston Blumenthal and Gordon Ramsay (whose own production company is behind the show). Catnip for 00s nostalgists.

The Greatest Prime Video, 4 November Boxing dramas are a Hollywood mainstay, but this year the genre is migrating to the small screen with the likes of Fightland, A Thousand Blows and this new Muhammad Ali biopic, whose first season chronicles the vertiginous early 1960s rise of the then Cassius Clay (Jaalen Best).

Allies in Exile BBC Four/iPlayer, 3 November , 10pm BBC Four’s Storyville strand has long brought the world’s best feature-length documentaries to television. Now briefer films will be showcased too, starting with this one following the arduous journey of two Syrian film-makers through the UK’s asylum system. An Unknown Substance, about the poisoning of a Russian politician, airs afterwards. R A

Staying in: Games

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Switch 2; out 5 November The only major game challenging GTA 6 this month is this lively, stylish remake of Nintendo’s 1998 adventure classic, in which series hero Link becomes a time traveller to save the land of Hyrule from evil warlock Ganondorf. A nostalgic treat for the ages.

Where the Seeds Fall PS5, Switch 2, PC; out 5 November An intriguing action adventure which follows the human inhabitants of a vast tree as they set out to descend its branches and rediscover the land they were once forced to flee. Part mystical role-playing game, part climbing challenge. Keith Stuart

Staying in: Albums

Ex:Re – Save As Out now With her band Daughter currently between albums, Elena Tonra returns to her Ex:Re solo moniker via this second album of textural alt-rock. Songs such as Sleep creep along with a hint of menace, while opener Radio Station spins off into a trippy road trip anthem.

DIIV – Zirp! Out now American alt-rock curios DIIV return with this AG Cook-produced fifth album. While steeped in their typically opaque, shoegazey textures, songs such as the pop-adjacent Kid and chunky lead single The Fountain dial up the melodies and frontman Zachary Cole Smith’s hushed vocals.

Chloe Qisha – Fantasize Out now After quitting a psychology degree for pop stardom, Malaysia-born, UK-based singer-songwriter Qisha found instant success with 2024’s sultry I Lied, I’m Sorry. She increases the sex chat on this debut album, specifically on gloriously overblown banger YDH, AKA young, dumb and horny.

The Big Moon – Forever Out now London quartet the Big Moon return with a sunnier take on their brand of indie rock. Created as an imaginary utopia after a period of upheaval in frontwoman Juliette Jackson’s life, songs such as the buoyant Three Things and Fun offer sweet solace. MC

Staying in: Brain food

Provocations Podcast For the numerically challenged, this new series hosted by Nihal Arthanayake is essential listening. Experts break down the big stories in finance, such as changes in lending policies and how technology can affect banking.

Interior Motives YouTube On the surface this video series looks like a flippant guessing game pairing pictures of domestic interiors with their owners, but it in fact uncovers fascinating truths about the ways our homes reveal our hidden selves.

Concorde: The Untold Story PBS America, 2 November , 8.40pm Encompassing everything from engineering breakthroughs to espionage and political hand-wringing, this film on the race to build the first supersonic airliner between Europe, the Soviet Union and the US makes for surprisingly engaging viewing. title_original: Producer Titles Can Be Bought, but Real Creative Producers Take Them for Themselves
editorial_title_zh: 制片人头衔可以买到，但真正的创意制片人是靠自己争取来的
editorial_excerpt_zh: 制片人艾莉森·欧文、卡拉·哈肯和劳伦·米勒·罗根向 IndieWire 讲述了在将电影和电视剧搬上银幕的过程中坚持不懈的重要性。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为 SCAD 萨凡纳电影节的一部分，IndieWire 的“电影制作未来”团队推出了“镜头背后”（Behind Their Lens）系列座谈会，邀请了 2026 年最令人瞩目的手艺人、导演和制片人。", "links": [{"text": "SCAD Savannah Film Festival", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/festivals/scad-film-festival-2026-full-lineup-revealed-1235220023/"}, {"text": "Future of Filmmaking", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/future-of-filmmaking/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在制片人座谈会上，《Tangles》制片人劳伦·米勒·罗根、《幽灵》与《名姝》制片人艾莉森·欧文以及《穿普拉达的女魔头》制片人卡拉·哈肯向学生和来宾畅谈了各种话题，从他们如何着手对剧本提出好的、有建设性的意见，到他们如何看待当前迅速整合的媒体格局以真正让项目落地。", "links": [{"text": "Tangles", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/festivals/seth-rogen-tangles-specificity-animated-middleburg-1235222534/"}, {"text": "Lauren Miller Rogen", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/babies-review-anna-kendrick-seth-rogen-1235216694/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但贯穿他们所有制作阶段工作的核心，是一种用意志力推动项目冲破道路上任何障碍和挑战的坚持。自他们涉足制片行业实际工作以来，这一点就一直如此。欧文谈到，她在制片方面的“学位”是一群大学生带给她的，但并非通过真正上大学获得。这一切只是始于与当时正在英国国家电影学校就读的某人的对话。", "links": [{"text": "Film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/GettyImages-1817497483.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "迈克尔·曼", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2302281050.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "佐治亚州萨凡纳 - 10月27日：（左起）索菲·隆瓦里、贝思·德·阿劳若、乔西·鲁克和斯蒂芬·格林于2026年10月27日在佐治亚州萨凡纳举行的第29届 SCAD 萨凡纳电影节期间，出席由 IndieWire 的“电影制作未来”呈现的“镜头背后：导演座谈会”并发言。（图片来源：Getty Images 供 SCAD 专用，摄影：辛迪·奥德）", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“那是80年代初，当时的情况要宽松得多，但他们说：‘那里没有制片人。但如果你想学习制片，就去诺丁山，早上巴士在科罗内特剧院外面停下时，你就站在那儿，上车就行了，’”欧文说。“你会被带到电影学校，那些正在制作毕业作品的学生会想找人来为他们制片。他们根本不在乎你以前没做过什么。我不知道什么是通告单，也不知道什么是制片助理或别的什么。但他们很高兴能多一双干活的手。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "愿意搭把手让欧文来到了威尔士中部的一个小村庄，参与一个大四毕业项目的制作，而那种深入一线的、极具外景地特色的工作，从那时起就为她奠定了良好的基础。“你不仅在学习东西，还在结识同龄人。所以他们都是后来执导主流电影厂大片的人、剪辑师、摄影师，比如现在和我合作的人——约翰·马西森，你知道的，我们以前都睡在酒吧楼上的床垫上，而他现在为乔·赖特掌镜，”欧文说。“我总是对学生说：‘与你的同行建立人脉。他们就是未来你会想要从他们那里获得工作或去雇用他们的人。’\"", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与同行的动态保持同步也能让你看到各种可能性。米勒·罗根几年前就写好了她的第一部长片剧本《为了好玩，打给我……》，但正是看到莉娜·杜汉姆在《微型家具》中的作品，才让她意识到这是她可以凭一己之力让其成为现实的事情。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我看了《微型家具》，我想：‘好吧，我也能做到。’于是我把电影从那个大制片人手里拿了回来，给我团队和编剧搭档发了封邮件，我说：‘我们要靠自己把它拍出来，而且我要亲自主演。’他们当时的反应是：‘哇。’而我说：‘不，这就是我们要做的，’”米勒·罗根说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种信念——再加上通过从事金融工作的米勒·罗根的哥哥结识的一些独立金主的关键人脉——为该片的预算筹集了75万美元。“我们拍摄了16天。然后我们去了圣丹斯，当然，能入选是很幸运的。但我们入选了圣丹斯，聚焦影业买下了它并发发行，它还上了院线，这在今天是绝对不会发生的。但这是非同寻常的，我当时感到震惊、骄傲和恐惧，因为它将变得规模庞大、广为人知，”米勒·罗根说。“但这太不可思议了，而且我认为现在有很多途径可以让你的项目被人看到。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我认为你刚才说得最对的一点是，对你们所有人来说，现在有很多途径可以让你们的作品问世，”哈肯补充道。“《后室》以及所有这些 YouTube 恐怖短片的成功应该给你们带来希望：你知道的，写出好东西，制作出好东西，找到一个好故事，除了过去那种方式，还有其他途径能把它拍出来。”", "translated": true}]

article_text:
As part of the SCAD Savannah Film Festival , IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking team presents “Behind Their Lens,” a series of panel discussions with some of the most exciting artisans, directors, and producers of 2026.

On the producers panel, “ Tangles ” producer Lauren Miller Rogen , “Ghosts” and “Harlots” producer Alison Owen, and “Devil Wears Prada” producer Carla Hacken spoke to students and guests about everything from how they approach giving good, productive notes on a story to how they’re looking at the current, rapidly consolidating media landscape for actually getting projects off the ground.

But the thing that unites all their work, across all phases of production, is a persistence to muscle it past whatever obstacles and challenges lie in its path. And that’s something that’s been true for them since they got into the actual work of the producing business. Owen spoke about how her “degree” in producing is something she earned with a bunch of university students, but not by actually attending university. It just started with a conversation with someone who was attending the UK’s National Film School at the time.

“This was the early ‘80s, when things were a lot looser, but they said, ‘There are no producers there. But if you want to learn about producing, go to Notting Hill, where the bus stops outside the Coronet in the morning and just stand there and get on the bus,” Owen said. “You would get out to the film school, and the students who were making their graduation films would want someone to come out and produce for them. And they didn’t care that you hadn’t done anything. I didn’t know what a call sheet was or what PAs were or anything. But they were happy to have a pair of hands.”

Being a willing pair of hands led Owen to a small village in the middle of Wales, working on a senior graduation project, and that on-the-ground, very-on-location work has stood her in good stead since. “Not only are you learning stuff, but you’re meeting your peers. So they were all people who wound up directing major studio movies, editors, cinematographers, people that I work with now, like John Mathieson, who — you know, we all slept on a mattress above a pub, and he now lights for Joe Wright,” Owen said. I always say to students, ‘Network with your peers. They’re the people of the future that you’re going to want to get jobs from or hire.”

Being tuned into what your peers are up to can also show you what’s possible. Miller Rogen had written the script for her first feature, “For A Good Time, Call…” years before, but it was seeing Lena Dunham’s work in “Tiny Furniture” that made her realize it was something she could make happen herself.

“I saw ‘Tiny Furniture,’ and I thought, ‘Well, I could do that.’ And so I took the movie from the big producer, and I emailed my team and my writing partner, and I said, ‘We’re gonna make this on our own, and I’m gonna star in it.’ And they were like, ‘Whoa.’ And I was like, ‘No, that’s what we’re doing,’” Miller Rogen said.

That conviction — and the key connections to some independent backers care of Miller Rogen’s brother who worked in finance — led to a $750,000 raise for the film’s budget. “We shot in 16 days. And then we went to Sundance, which is, of course, lucky to get into. But we got into Sundance and Focus Features bought it and released it, and it was in movie theaters, which would never happen now. But it was extraordinary, and I felt shock and pride and fear because it was gonna be big and out there,” Rogen Miller said. “But it was incredible, and I think these days, there are so many ways to get your project seen.”

“ I think you just said the most important thing for all of them is there’s so many ways for you guys to get your work out there now,” Hacken added. “The success of ‘Backrooms’ and all these YouTube horror shows should give you hope that, you know, write something good, produce something good, find a great story, and there are other ways to get it made than the way it used to be.”
excerpt_original: Producers Alison Owen, Carla Hacken, and Lauren Miller Rogen tell IndieWire about the importance of persistence in bringing films and TV shows to life.

title_original: ‘Street Fighter’ Review: Video Game Fighter Film Knocks Itself Unconscious
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "You could set your watch to the moment Kitao Sakurai ’s “ Street Fighter ” stops working. It’s almost exactly at the halfway mark, when its streamlined, delightfully cartoonish saga actually reaches its central tournament, an elimination series of seven fights, of which we see maybe one and a half. From that point on, this martial arts video game adaptation becomes disastrously scattered, between setups and payoffs at complete odds, confounding ADR, and a total lack of any actual conclusion. (Photo by Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images)", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "'My Brilliant Career' Star Philippa Northeast Replaces Quintessa Swindell in Netflix Drama 'Feral' (EXCLUSIVE)", "links": [{"text": "'My Brilliant Career' Star Philippa Northeast Replaces Quintessa Swindell in Netflix Drama 'Feral' (EXCLUSIVE)", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/tv/news/philippa-northeast-replaces-quintessa-swindell-feral-netflix-1236918673/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The movie’s masterstroke is an introduction (and several subsequent flashbacks) rendered in 2D animation, courtesy of studio Titmouse Inc. These fiery, anime-inspired segments set the stage for the story of video game mainstays Ken ( Noah Centineo ) and Ryu (Andrew Koji), American and Japanese best friends who train under the stern sensei Gouken (Don Lee). Ryu was the winner of the first ever World Warrior tournament in 1987, a victory that led him to the edge of dark, all-consuming powers, courtesy of Gouken’s demonic brother Akuma (pro wrestler Joe “Roman Reigns” Anoa’i), a figure lurking in the shadows.", "links": [{"text": "Noah Centineo", "url": "https://variety.com/t/noah-centineo/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Upon moving into live action, “Street Fighter” takes a less serious tone, albeit a consistently funny one, via stylized MTV clips recapping Ken’s reckless stardom and Ryu’s self-imposed exile after Gouken’s demise. Six years later, as Ken wins staged fights with the help of opportunistic manager Dan Hibiki (comedian Andrew Schulz, the film’s soulful secret weapon), and Ryu quietly runs a failing noodle stall, they’re approached by secret Interpol agent Chun-Li (Callina Liang). She invites them to a revived World Warrior tournament courtesy of her target, the fascistically-styled Lord M. Bison (David Dastmalchian), who seeks to harness a force called “Psycho Power” from its winner."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These ludicrous ideas are dramatized through appropriately silly scenes where action is the default lingua franca. It’s an approach verging on professional wrestling (fitting, for a film starring at least three pro wrestlers), wherein fisticuffs stand in for everything from negotiations to brotherly reunions. Ken is eager to win the aforementioned tournament, while Ryu is cautious about the ulterior motives for its staging, leading to a surprisingly meaningful tension between the former besties, as they check into M. Bison’s gilded hotel and cross paths with the other fighters — friends and foes alike."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This leads to even more behind-the-scenes skirmishes laced with character-centric comedy, as opposing factions align. On one side stands M. Bison’s forces — the boxer Balrog (rapper Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson), the odorous, green-skinned lightning monster Blanka ( Jason Momoa ), and the suave, claw-wielding Vega (masked country musician Orville Peck) — while the de facto “good” side features American G.I. article_text:
You could set your watch to the moment Kitao Sakurai ’s “ Street Fighter ” stops working. It’s almost exactly at the halfway mark, when its streamlined, delightfully cartoonish saga actually reaches its central tournament, an elimination series of seven fights, of which we see maybe one and a half. From that point on, this martial arts video game adaptation becomes disastrously scattered, between setups and payoffs at complete odds, confounding ADR, and a total lack of any actual conclusion. It’s a shame, given how enjoyable the film initially is.

Related Stories

'My Brilliant Career' Star Philippa Northeast Replaces Quintessa Swindell in Netflix Drama 'Feral' (EXCLUSIVE)

The movie’s masterstroke is an introduction (and several subsequent flashbacks) rendered in 2D animation, courtesy of studio Titmouse Inc. These fiery, anime-inspired segments set the stage for the story of video game mainstays Ken ( Noah Centineo ) and Ryu (Andrew Koji), American and Japanese best friends who train under the stern sensei Gouken (Don Lee). Ryu was the winner of the first ever World Warrior tournament in 1987, a victory that led him to the edge of dark, all-consuming powers, courtesy of Gouken’s demonic brother Akuma (pro wrestler Joe “Roman Reigns” Anoa’i), a figure lurking in the shadows.

Upon moving into live action, “Street Fighter” takes a less serious tone, albeit a consistently funny one, via stylized MTV clips recapping Ken’s reckless stardom and Ryu’s self-imposed exile after Gouken’s demise. Six years later, as Ken wins staged fights with the help of opportunistic manager Dan Hibiki (comedian Andrew Schulz, the film’s soulful secret weapon), and Ryu quietly runs a failing noodle stall, they’re approached by secret Interpol agent Chun-Li (Callina Liang). She invites them to a revived World Warrior tournament courtesy of her target, the fascistically-styled Lord M. Bison (David Dastmalchian), who seeks to harness a force called “Psycho Power” from its winner.

These ludicrous ideas are dramatized through appropriately silly scenes where action is the default lingua franca. It’s an approach verging on professional wrestling (fitting, for a film starring at least three pro wrestlers), wherein fisticuffs stand in for everything from negotiations to brotherly reunions. Ken is eager to win the aforementioned tournament, while Ryu is cautious about the ulterior motives for its staging, leading to a surprisingly meaningful tension between the former besties, as they check into M. Bison’s gilded hotel and cross paths with the other fighters — friends and foes alike.

This leads to even more behind-the-scenes skirmishes laced with character-centric comedy, as opposing factions align. On one side stands M. Bison’s forces — the boxer Balrog (rapper Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson), the odorous, green-skinned lightning monster Blanka ( Jason Momoa ), and the suave, claw-wielding Vega (masked country musician Orville Peck) — while the de facto “good” side features American G.I. Guile (wrestler Cody Rhodes) and mystic fighter Dhalsim (Indian martial artist Vidyut Jammwal). However, the deft combination of punchy dialogue, tongue-in-cheek stunt casting and formally audacious video game effects paves the path for a second half that doesn’t remotely cohere.

As the film becomes increasingly split between the tournament and M. Bison’s unraveling conspiracy, something goes terribly awry in its back half, hinting at either a troubled production, or one that was doomed from the start. The dialogue, whether expository exchanges or quippy one-liners, grows splintered, and is increasingly presented with the backs of speakers’ heads or their mouths partially obscured; it would be interesting to learn how much of the film was rewritten in post.

Worse yet, the movie starts to cut away from its heightened action just as quickly, replacing it with awkward, seemingly improvised comedy that seldom lands (some of it from a TV presenter played by miscast Eric André, Sakurai’s long-time collaborator). That is, when the dialogue is audible at all; much of it ends up subsumed by a thundering sound mix that obscures what you’re actually meant to hear.

The film’s biggest sin, however, is stringing its characters along through a plot that adds vital story elements through flashbacks well over an hour in (such as Ryu and Ken’s secret energy abilities, and the meaning behind them), as they tumble toward inevitable conclusions which never actually materialize. “Street Fighter” has two main antagonists in M. Bison and Akuma, both of whom mostly wait around as the tournament unfolds so they can take advantage of its winner, but neither of whom seems aware of the other’s presence or intentions. So, when it comes time to weave all these threads together (including Chun-Li’s vengeful arc against M. Bison), every character ends up with the wrong emotional climax, and things simply peter out without a real finale.

The film often pays homage to the fan favorite “Street Fighter II: The Animated Movie” (which, despite its title, isn’t actually a sequel), and while this results in some seamless fan service like the occasional bit of throwback dialogue, it also yields a number of awkward scenes left hanging in mid-air. One such moment is, in fact, the film’s conclusion, which is similarly open-ended, but without earning enough goodwill to promise a sequel. Another is a scene of Chun-Li entering a steamy shower. In the animated movie, this led to a vulnerable fight against Vega, with the Interpol agent on the backfoot; even though it was patently salacious, it also served a purpose within the story.

However, the same can’t be said of a similar moment in the live action “Street Fighter,” where the camera simply leers at Liang’s body in a transitionary moment. That the actress put in the work to match the character’s muscular physique is no doubt impressive, but the number of stray shots of women’s buttocks makes the film feel uncomfortable retrograde. (Not to mention several jokes where the punchline is Guile’s latent queerness.)

What little emotional maturity “Street Fighter” appears to display in its initial half goes flying out the window, alongside all sense of story or character, in its second. It’s a film at war with itself, in which a straightforward narrative about strained brotherhood is spread far too thin across unconnected snippets of action and comedy that grow increasingly disparate. And while its major strength remains its hand-drawn flashbacks, the more its two-hour run time proceeds, the more it feels like this captivating anime version of the classic arcade game ought to have been the main event in the first place.

‘Street Fighter’ Review: Video Game Fighter Film Knocks Itself Unconscious

article_text:
Ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3, all eyes are on the White House, specifically its interiors.

After White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino posted a video on X of the construction of President Donald Trump ’s ballroom on Friday, former President Barack Obama told a crowd at an Ohio rally on Saturday gave his opinion on the video. “I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation. He should be on HGTV,” Obama said, adding that Trump is building a “ballroom that’s bigger than the White House” and questioning “What’s with all the gold? He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened up a Cheesecake Factory.”

Obama wasn’t the only one criticizing Trump’s taste for lavish interiors. At a rally on Friday in Hollywood, Florida, former President Bill Clinton also mocked the refurbishments taking place at the White House. “I think Congress made a mistake not protesting turning the Rose Garden into what looks like the entrance to Liberace’s bathroom,” he said.

In September, a divided Supreme Court ruled that Trump’s luxury ballroom will proceed as planned and replace the East Wing of the White House. The court ruled in a 5-to-4 vote that the National Trust for Historic Preservation, a nonprofit chartered by Congress, did not have the legal grounds to bring its lawsuit because the persons in question were not directly harmed by the project.

“This is not the final decision on the merits of our case and does not resolve our fundamental argument—that each president is a temporary steward of the People’s House and does not have the unilateral authority to demolish and redesign it without the approval of Congress,” National Trust president Brent Leggs said at the time.

article_text:
I t’s likely that most audiences going into the surprise documentary smash You Can See Everything are familiar with either its nominal subject (and literal poster gal with an intense stare) Elizabeth Holmes, the tech founder serving a prison sentence for defrauding investors; or the film’s on-camera co-director Nathan Fielder. Holmes, as the movie points out, was all over the media as her company Theranos was hyped to the moon and then spectacularly imploded; she was also played by Amanda Seyfried in the well-regarded Hulu miniseries The Dropout. Fielder, meanwhile, may not have graced as many magazine covers, but is similarly familiar to prestige-TV acolytes from his comedy-reality series Nathan for You and its successor, the more reality-bending series The Rehearsal. A third figure not included in the film’s ad campaign becomes a key part of the film in the second half, and will also be familiar to many viewers.

This should leave Billy Evans as the odd man out. Evans, Elizabeth Holmes’s partner (she has said they’re not legally married, though they did get engaged in 2018, have two children and seem to treat each other as spouses), is a not-particularly-famous guy whose screen time competes with the other three well-known faces in what is essentially a four-character drama. But while Evans isn’t boxed out in terms of screen time or memorability, he does remain the odd man out in the sense that in all the discussion You Can See Everything has prompted about manipulation, shifting sympathies and who can or cannot be trusted, everyone seems to agree on one crucial point: Billy Evans sucks.

Well, everyone except Holmes, who never indicates so much as a moment of doubt or hesitation toward her common-law husband, at least so far as Fielder or co-director Lance Oppenheim show us. But the movie does show Fielder appearing baffled by Holmes – her absurd claims to have never lied in her adult life; her tautological and nonsensical explanation of how her blood-testing device does actually work (which basically amounts to “if everything about it worked, it would work”); her inability to understand Abbott and Costello’s most famous comedy routine – to the point of having trouble discerning whether she’s consciously scamming him or just, let’s say, reality-divergent. By comparison, Evans comes across as more of a slightly puzzling but recognizable nuisance.

When he calls a meeting to demand a percentage of the film’s profits – the kind of arrangement that might be typically reserved for a promotional piece commissioned by a musician, not a nonfiction film extensively interviewing a notorious subject – Fielder and Oppenheim zero in on the question of whether Holmes knew about this request and what became of it, but Evans is the one who violates documentary norms by asking for profit participation (and getting it, at least temporarily). Earlier on, he demands privacy when he grows visibly uncomfortable with questions asked of Holmes while also appearing fully, frontally nude in the film. In a small but underlined moment, he casually relieves Holmes of egg-scrambling duty because he believes she’s not stirring vigorously enough.

And those are just some of his antics before the film’s two-year time jump, after which Evans seems to exert even more control over his partner. Given Holmes’s reputation as a Silicon Valley scam artist, it would make sense enough to categorize Evans as a real-life version of Hollywood’s favorite go-to villain: the evil tech bro . The film even refers to Holmes’s turn in that particular hot seat as the subject of The Dropout, which is not a story of heroes and villains, exactly, but certainly exists adjacent to narratives about tech-forward monsters.

Evans has plenty of grimly hilarious signifiers, before and after his partner’s incarceration. Beforehand, he can be seen listening to podcasts at double speed like a true #content consumer/wannabe timemaxxer. Afterward, he shows repeated signs (uncommented upon by Oppenheim or Fielder) of posturing but increasingly intense post-“woke” radicalization: he spends time at a shooting range, claims to carry a gun everywhere, volunteers that he’s a fan of Charlie Kirk and brags about his own supposed vindictiveness. He uses his sketchy control of Holmes’s social media to engage in petty clapbacks that seem entirely out of character for her; he uses his sketchy control of her AI likeness to side-boast about how much healthier she looks as a prisoner than she did immediately postpartum.

With paranoia, delusions of grandeur, lofty-sounding projects that don’t amount to anything and a seeming possessiveness of the woman in his life, Evans checks plenty of tech-bro boxes – only without even a modicum of demonstrated tech expertise, seemingly not even in his fevered imaginings. Yes, Elon Musk propped himself up as a genius on the basis of other people’s companies and his vast fortune; Mark Zuckerberg is a dead-eyed egomaniac whose famous invention is a Friendster clone that bought up a bunch of other already-successful websites and Sam Altman’s career is littered with failures that in no way qualify him to order us all to treat AI as the future. But even if you see these guys as scammers nearly on par with Holmes, they have the distinction of having successfully made money and, in the case of Musk and Zuckerberg, placing some of their might behind products that people do actually use (in some cases, whether they really want to or not). One reason they’re villainized in fictionalized true stories like those powering The Social Reckoning (with Jeremy Strong as Zuck) or the upcoming Artificial (with Andrew Garfield as Altman and Ike Barinholtz as Musk) is that they have actually accrued power in the first place. There are stakes to their existence.

Evans has no such claims to fame or even big-canvas notoriety that could inspire something like the four-hour Musk documentary by Alex Gibney, released concurrently with You Can See Everything. It seems notable, too, that the similarly lengthy You Can See Everything has seemingly stolen focus from the more traditionally rigorous piece on Musk, a far more influential individual compared to either Holmes or Evans. Holmes was certainly a destructive force for the cancer patients whose hopes she raised, and Evans comes across like a restless creep, but it feels telling, and a little discomfiting, that the gossipy nervous laughter provoked by You Can See Everything is proving a vastly more headline-grabbing draw than a movie laying out the case against a maniacal on-again, off-again trillionaire who has done genuine damage to the world, and is poised to do plenty more. Does someone need to be as petty, strange and blatantly unsuccessful as Evans to be truly finished off in public?

Then again, Evans does make a compelling villain for precisely that restless lack of achievement. He will never be as influential as someone like Musk or Zuckerberg, but apparently aspires to that kind of overlord-level bravado (why else would you use your wife’s social media to pick fights?). He’s a fake-it-til-you-make-it-and-then-keeping-faking-it type, more akin to erstwhile reality star turned pretend mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt or any number of filibustering podcasters. Instead of Facebook or Tesla or a portfolio of Donald Trump-style scams, he can simply puppeteer the damaged brand that is Elizabeth Holmes – near-literally, when he shows off his AI version. Holmes is clearly manipulative (and based on available information about Theranos, an unambiguous liar), yet Fielder does locate, or maybe even manufacture, some kind of humanity through her inscrutability. There’s something haunting about her, sometimes in spite of herself. Evans is the odd man out in You Can See Everything because he seems to lack that kind of turmoil. He’s hustle-and-grind culture in its final dehumanizing form. The world is just something for him to absorb and scan for advantages at 2x speed.

article_text:
Shooting is underway in Venice on “ Upgraded 2,” the sequel to Amazon MGM Studios’ buzzy 2024 rom-com “Upgraded” that, as announced, is set to star Leslie Bibb alongside Camila Mendes .

Mendes is returning to the franchise as Ana Santos, an intern at a New York City auction house who feigns a higher job status after she is upgraded to first class on her flight to London. During the flight, she impresses a wealthy young Englishman named William who is connected to the high-society art world, played by Archie Renaux.

Related Stories

Disney Names Carol Choi Asia Pacific President as Luke Kang Retires

In the sequel to the modern-day “Cinderella” tale, on which cameras started rolling in Venice on Oct. 21, Ana is now seemingly seeking to make her mark at the Venice Biennale art exhibition, the world’s oldest contemporary art fair. Becca Gleason, who is helming the sequel — taking over from “Upgraded” director Carlson Young — has been shooting on the terrace of Ca’ Giustinian, the Biennale headquarters that overlook the lagoon’s Grand Canal; in the neo-Gothic Palazzo Franchetti near the Accademia bridge, which serves as a Biennale exhibition space; and at the luxurious Moro Venice restaurant. So far, there are no indications on what Bibb’s role is.

Luke Roberts and Justin Matthews, who penned the first film, also wrote the screenplay for the sequel.

Besides Venice and the Biennale, “Upgraded 2″ will have a decidedly Italian flavor. Following 12 days of shooting on the lagoon, principal photography will move to Rome where 33 more days of shooting are planned, according to Italy for Movies, the country’s national portal for film and TV production locations and incentives. The production designer is Italy’s Luca Tranchino (“Prison Break,” “Domina”). The Italian company serving as executive producer on the sequel is Colorado Film.

Producers on “Upgraded 2″ include Mike Karz and Bill Bindley for Gulfstream Pictures, Mendes and Rachel Matthews for Honor Role, Lena Roklin for Luber Roklin Entertainment and Piers Tempest for Tempo Production.
